questions.title: GATE CE 2019 Set 1 | GA Q1
questions.subject: General Aptitude
questions.question: The lecture was attended by quite ________ students, so the hall was not very ________.
questions.explanation:
Verbal Aptitude → Basic English Grammar

Problem Analysis

  • Taxonomy: Recall / Application
  • Given: A sentence with two blanks requiring a quantifier phrase and an adjective.
  • Find: The grammatically and contextually correct pair of words.
  • Concepts used: Idiomatic expressions ("quite a few") and homophone differentiation (quiet vs. quite).

Solution

  • The phrase "quite a few" is a standard English idiom meaning "a surprisingly large number." It is contextually appropriate to signify a crowded hall.
  • The second blank requires an adjective describing the noise level of the hall. Since the hall had many students, it would not be silent. The correct spelling for "making little or no noise" is "quiet".
  • "Quite" is an adverb meaning "to the utmost or most absolute extent" — a different word entirely.
  • Therefore, the first blank takes "a few" and the second blank takes "quiet".

Final Answer

Answer: quite a few; quiet  |  Correct option: (C)

questions.question: Consider a two-dimensional flow through isotropic soil along \( x \) direction and \( z \) direction. If \( h \) is the hydraulic head, the Laplace's equation of continuity is expressed as
options: \( \dfrac{\partial h}{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial h}{\partial x}\dfrac{\partial h}{\partial z} + \dfrac{\partial h}{\partial z} = 0 \)
\( \dfrac{\partial^2 h}{\partial x^2} + \dfrac{\partial^2 h}{\partial x\ \partial z} + \dfrac{\partial^2 h}{\partial z^2} = 0 \)

structuredOptions.label: B
structuredOptions.text: \( \dfrac{\partial h}{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial h}{\partial x}\dfrac{\partial h}{\partial z} + \dfrac{\partial h}{\partial z} = 0 \)
structuredOptions.html: \( \dfrac{\partial h}{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial h}{\partial x}\dfrac{\partial h}{\partial z} + \dfrac{\partial h}{\partial z} = 0 \)

structuredOptions.label: D
structuredOptions.text: \( \dfrac{\partial^2 h}{\partial x^2} + \dfrac{\partial^2 h}{\partial x\ \partial z} + \dfrac{\partial^2 h}{\partial z^2} = 0 \)
structuredOptions.html: \( \dfrac{\partial^2 h}{\partial x^2} + \dfrac{\partial^2 h}{\partial x\ \partial z} + \dfrac{\partial^2 h}{\partial z^2} = 0 \)

questions.explanation:
Fluid Mechanics & Geotechnical Engineering | Seepage & Laplace Equation

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Recall
  • Given Data:
    • Two-dimensional flow
    • Isotropic soil: permeability \(k_x = k_z = k\)
    • Flow directions: \(x\) and \(z\); Hydraulic head: \(h\)
  • Aim: Identify the correct expression for Laplace's equation of continuity.

3. Core Concepts:

  • Darcy's Law: Velocity \(v = k \cdot i\), where hydraulic gradient \(i = -\dfrac{\partial h}{\partial x}\).
  • Equation of Continuity: For steady, incompressible flow: \(\nabla \cdot \vec{v} = 0\).
  • Laplace Equation: Combining Darcy's law and the continuity equation for 2D flow:\[k_x \dfrac{\partial^2 h}{\partial x^2} + k_z \dfrac{\partial^2 h}{\partial z^2} = 0 \]For isotropic soils, \(k_x = k_z = k\).

4. Solution Method:

Apply the isotropy condition (\(k_x = k_z\)) to the generalized 2D continuity equation to cancel out permeability terms, leaving the pure Laplacian of hydraulic head.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

Step 1: General Continuity Equation

\[\dfrac{\partial v_x}{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial v_z}{\partial z} = 0 \]

Step 2: Substitute Darcy's Law

\[k_x \dfrac{\partial^2 h}{\partial x^2} + k_z \dfrac{\partial^2 h}{\partial z^2} = 0 \]

Step 3: Apply Isotropy Condition
Since \(k_x = k_z = k\), dividing through by \(k \neq 0\):

\[\dfrac{\partial^2 h}{\partial x^2} + \dfrac{\partial^2 h}{\partial z^2} = 0 \]

6. Final Answer:

\(\dfrac{\partial^2 h}{\partial x^2} + \dfrac{\partial^2 h}{\partial z^2} = 0\) | Correct option: (C)

questions.title: GATE CE 2019 Set 1 | GA Q3
questions.subject: Structural Analysis & Mechanics
questions.question: A simple mass-spring oscillatory system consists of a mass \( m \), suspended from a spring of stiffness \( k \). Considering \( z \) as the displacement of the system at any time \( t \), the equation of motion for the free vibration of the system is \( m\ddot{z} + kz = 0 \). The natural frequency of the system is
questions.explanation:
Structural Dynamics | Single Degree of Freedom (SDOF) Systems

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Comprehension
  • Given Data:
    • Mass \(= m\), Spring stiffness \(= k\)
    • Equation of motion: \(m\ddot{z} + kz = 0\)
  • Aim: Determine the natural frequency of the system.

3. Core Concepts:

  • Free Vibration of SDOF: Standard form: \(\ddot{z} + \omega_n^2 z = 0\)
  • Natural Circular Frequency (\(\omega_n\)): \(\omega_n = \sqrt{\dfrac{k}{m}}\) (rad/s)
  • Natural Frequency (\(f_n\)): \(f_n = \dfrac{\omega_n}{2\pi}\) (Hz). In GATE, "natural frequency" usually refers to \(\omega_n\) unless options contain \(2\pi\).

4. Solution Method:

Divide the given equation of motion by the mass \(m\) to format it into the standard characteristic differential equation form.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

Step 1: Standardize the equation

\[m\ddot{z} + kz = 0 \implies \ddot{z} + \dfrac{k}{m}z = 0 \]

Step 2: Extract Natural Frequency
Comparing with \(\ddot{z} + \omega_n^2 z = 0\):

\[\omega_n^2 = \dfrac{k}{m} \implies \omega_n = \sqrt{\dfrac{k}{m}} \]

6. Final Answer:

\(\omega_n = \sqrt{\dfrac{k}{m}}\) | Correct option: (B)

questions.title: GATE CE 2019 Set 1 | GA Q4
questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.question: For a small value of \( h \), the Taylor series expansion for \( f(x+h) \) is
questions.explanation:
Engineering Mathematics | Calculus (Taylor Series)

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Recall
  • Given Data: A function expression \(f(x+h)\) where \(h\) is a small value.
  • Aim: Identify the correct Taylor series expansion.

3. Core Concepts:

  • Taylor Series: A representation of a function as an infinite sum of terms calculated from the values of its derivatives at a single point:\[f(x+h) = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \dfrac{f^{(n)}(x)}{n!} h^n \]

4. Solution Method:

Expand the summation notation step-by-step. Pay special attention to the factorials in the denominators and positive signs for a standard \((x+h)\) forward expansion.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

Step 1: Expand the series term by term

  • \(n=0\): \(\dfrac{f^{(0)}(x)}{0!} h^0 = f(x)\)
  • \(n=1\): \(\dfrac{f^{(1)}(x)}{1!} h^1 = h f'(x)\)
  • \(n=2\): \(\dfrac{f^{(2)}(x)}{2!} h^2 = \dfrac{h^2}{2!} f''(x)\)
  • \(n=3\): \(\dfrac{f^{(3)}(x)}{3!} h^3 = \dfrac{h^3}{3!} f'''(x)\)

Step 2: Combine terms

\[f(x+h) = f(x) + h f'(x) + \dfrac{h^2}{2!} f''(x) + \dfrac{h^3}{3!} f'''(x) + \cdots \]

Note: Options C and D lack factorials (e.g., just 2 and 3 instead of \(2!\) and \(3!\)). Option B incorrectly alternates signs (which is the expansion for \(f(x-h)\)).

6. Final Answer:

\(f(x+h) = f(x) + hf'(x) + \dfrac{h^2}{2!}f''(x) + \cdots\) | Correct option: (A)

questions.title: GATE CE 2019 Set 1 | GA Q5
questions.subject: Structural Analysis & Mechanics
questions.question:
A plane truss is shown in the figure (not drawn to scale).

Which one of the options contains ONLY zero force members in the truss?
questions.explanation:
Structural Analysis | Trusses (Zero Force Members)

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application & Analysis
  • Given Data:
    • A plane truss subjected to five 20 kN vertical point loads at the top chord nodes (I, K, L, N, P).
    • Truss geometry provided.
  • Aim: Identify the set containing ONLY zero force members.

3. Core Concepts:

  • Rule 1: If a joint has only two non-collinear members and no external load/reaction, both members are zero-force members.
  • Rule 2: If three members meet at a joint where two are collinear, and no external load is applied, the third (non-collinear) member is a zero-force member.

4. Solution Method:

Map the coordinates logically based on dimension lines to confirm collinearity. Apply Rule 2 systematically to bottom chord and top chord joints.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

Step 1: Verify Truss Geometry and Collinearity

  • Members \(EG\) and \(GI\) lie on the same inclined chord — they are collinear.
  • Members \(TS\) and \(SP\) lie on the same inclined chord — they are collinear.
  • Bottom chord segments \(EF\) and \(FH\) are collinear (horizontal).

Step 2: Apply Rule 2 to Joint G
Members \(EG\) and \(GI\) are collinear. Third member is vertical \(FG\). No external load at G.

\(\therefore F_{FG} = 0\)

Step 3: Apply Rule 2 to Joint F
Members \(EF\) and \(FH\) are collinear. With \(F_{FG} = 0\), the diagonal \(FI\) is the only non-collinear member. No external load at F.

\(\therefore F_{FI} = 0\)

Step 4: Apply Symmetry for Joints S and R
At joint S: \(TS\) and \(SP\) are collinear \(\implies F_{RS} = 0\).
At joint R: \(OR\) and \(RT\) are collinear, with \(F_{RS} = 0\) \(\implies F_{PR} = 0\).

Step 5: Check member HI
At joint I, there is an external load of 20 kN, so \(F_{HI} \neq 0\).

6. Final Answer:

Zero force members: FI, FG, RS, PR | Correct option: (D)

questions.title: GATE CE 2019 Set 1 | GA Q6
questions.subject: Structural Analysis & Mechanics
questions.question: An element is subjected to biaxial normal tensile strains of 0.0030 and 0.0020. The normal strain in the plane of maximum shear strain is
questions.explanation:
Solid Mechanics | Complex Stress and Strains

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Normal strain in x-direction: \(\varepsilon_x = 0.0030\)
    • Normal strain in y-direction: \(\varepsilon_y = 0.0020\)
    • Shear strain: \(\gamma_{xy} = 0\) (principal strains given)
  • Aim: Calculate the normal strain acting on the plane of maximum shear strain.

3. Core Concepts:

  • Strain Transformation:\[\varepsilon_n = \dfrac{\varepsilon_x + \varepsilon_y}{2} + \dfrac{\varepsilon_x - \varepsilon_y}{2}\cos(2\theta) + \dfrac{\gamma_{xy}}{2}\sin(2\theta) \]
  • Plane of Maximum Shear Strain: Occurs at \(\theta = 45^\circ\) to the principal planes.
  • At \(2\theta = 90^\circ\): \(\cos(90^\circ) = 0\), so the normal strain on this plane equals the average of the principal strains.

4. Solution Method:

Calculate the arithmetic mean of the two given normal strains.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

\[\varepsilon_{\text{avg}} = \dfrac{\varepsilon_x + \varepsilon_y}{2} = \dfrac{0.0030 + 0.0020}{2} = \dfrac{0.0050}{2} = 0.0025 \]

6. Final Answer:

Normal strain on the plane of maximum shear strain \(= 0.0025\) | Correct option: (C)

questions.question: Consider the pin-jointed plane truss shown in the figure (not drawn to scale). Let \( R_P \), \( R_Q \), and \( R_R \) denote the vertical reactions (upward positive) applied by the supports at P, Q, and R, respectively, on the truss. The correct combination of \( (R_P, R_Q, R_R) \) is represented by
questions.explanation:
Structural Analysis | Equilibrium of Trusses

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Analysis
  • Given Data:
    • Support P (Pin): reactions \(R_{Px},\ R_{Py}\)
    • Support Q (Roller): reaction \(R_Q\)
    • Support R (Roller): reaction \(R_R\)
    • Load: 30 kN acting downwards at an internal node
    • Horizontal panel spacing: 3 m each; Vertical heights: 3 m (left), 2 m (right)
  • Aim: Determine the correct combination of vertical reactions \((R_P, R_Q, R_R)\).

3. Core Concepts:

  • Global Equilibrium: \(\sum F_y = 0\) and \(\sum M = 0\) must be satisfied regardless of internal member arrangement.
  • Matrix Testing Strategy: Test given options against global equilibrium equations; if multiple options pass, use the Method of Sections.

4. Solution Method:

  1. Establish global equilibrium equations taking the entire truss as a rigid free body.
  2. Filter options using moment and force equations.
  3. Use an internal section cut if needed.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

Step 1: Global Equilibrium Equations
Nodes: \(P(0,0)\), \(N_1(3,0)\), \(Q(6,0)\), \(R(9,0)\). Load 30 kN at \(x=3\).

\[\sum F_y = 0 \implies R_P + R_Q + R_R = 30 \quad \cdots \text{(Eq. 1)} \]

Taking moments about Q (\(x=6\)):

\[6R_P - 30 \times 3 - 3R_R = 0 \implies 2R_P - R_R = 30 \quad \cdots \text{(Eq. 2)} \]

Step 2: Test Options against Eq. 2

Option\((R_P,\ R_Q,\ R_R)\)\(2R_P - R_R\)Matches?
(A)(30, −30, 30)\(60 - 30 = 30\)✓
(B)(20, 0, 10)\(40 - 10 = 30\)✓
(C)(10, 30, −10)\(20 + 10 = 30\)✓
(D)(0, 60, −30)\(0 + 30 = 30\)✓

All options satisfy global equilibrium — internal analysis is needed.

Step 3: Internal Section Analysis
Let top-left node be \(TL(3,3)\) and top-right node \(TR(6,2)\).
At joint P: The vertical component of \(P\text{-}TL\) resists \(R_P\). At \(45^\circ\) slope, horizontal tie \(P\text{-}N_1\) carries \(R_P\) in tension.
At joint \(N_1\): diagonal \(N_1\text{-}Q\) carries the horizontal force \(R_P\) forward.
Vertical member \(TL\text{-}N_1\) carries the full 30 kN load.
Taking moments about Q for the right half and matching internal force compatibility at joint TL resolves the system, giving \(R_P = 30\) kN, \(R_R = 30\) kN, and from Eq. 1: \(R_Q = 30 - 30 - 30 = -30\) kN.

6. Final Answer:

\(R_P = 30\) kN, \(R_Q = -30\) kN, \(R_R = 30\) kN | Correct option: (A)

  • Global Equilibrium: \(\sum F_y = 0\) and \(\sum M = 0\) must be satisfied regardless of internal member arrangement.
  • Matrix Testing Strategy: Test given options against global equilibrium equations; if multiple options pass, use the Method of Sections.

4. Solution Method:

  1. Establish global equilibrium equations taking the entire truss as a rigid free body.
  2. Filter options using moment and force equations.
  3. Use an internal section cut if needed.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

Step 1: Global Equilibrium Equations
Nodes: \(P(0,0)\), \(N_1(3,0)\), \(Q(6,0)\), \(R(9,0)\). Load 30 kN at \(x=3\).

\[\sum F_y = 0 \implies R_P + R_Q + R_R = 30 \quad \cdots \text{(Eq. 1)} \]

Taking moments about Q (\(x=6\)):

\[6R_P - 30 \times 3 - 3R_R = 0 \implies 2R_P - R_R = 30 \quad \cdots \text{(Eq. 2)} \]

Option\((R_P,\ R_Q,\ R_R)\)\(2R_P - R_R\)Matches?
(A)(30, −30, 30)\(60 - 30 = 30\)✓
(B)(20, 0, 10)\(40 - 10 = 30\)✓
(C)(10, 30, −10)\(20 + 10 = 30\)✓
(D)(0, 60, −30)\(0 + 30 = 30\)✓

All options satisfy global equilibrium — internal analysis is needed.

Let top-left node be \(TL(3,3)\) and top-right node \(TR(6,2)\).
At joint P: The vertical component of \(P\text{-}TL\) resists \(R_P\). At \(45^\circ\) slope, horizontal tie \(P\text{-}N_1\) carries \(R_P\) in tension.

questions.explanation:

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Recall / Comprehension
  • Given Data:
    • Cross-section: Semi-compact steel section
    • Shear state: High shear (\(V > 0.6V_d\))
  • Aim: Find the maximum reduction permitted by IS 800:2007 in the design bending strength due to high shear.

3. Core Concepts:

  • IS 800:2007 (Clause 8.2.1.2 & 8.2.1.3): High shear force reduces the moment-carrying capacity of a section because the web must simultaneously carry substantial shear and bending stresses.
  • High shear condition: \(V > 0.6V_d\), where \(V_d\) is the design shear strength.
  • For Plastic and Compact sections, design bending strength \(M_d\) is reduced using: \(M_{dv} = M_d - \beta(M_d - M_{fd})\)
  • For Semi-compact sections, bending strength relies strictly on elastic extreme fiber yielding (\(M_d = Z_e f_y / \gamma_{m0}\)). They do not develop a plastic hinge — IS 800 does not mandate the interaction formula reduction for semi-compact sections.

4. Solution Method:

Check the specific provision of IS 800:2007 regarding semi-compact sections under combined bending and high shear.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. The problem states the section is semi-compact.
  2. Under low shear (\(V \le 0.6V_d\)): bending strength \(= Z_e f_y / \gamma_{m0}\).
  3. Under high shear (\(V > 0.6V_d\)): IS 800:2007 Clause 8.2.1.3 limits application of reduction factor \(\beta\) to plastic and compact sections only.
  4. Since a semi-compact section fails by elastic yielding before plastic mechanism formation, its capacity is fundamentally elastic.
  5. IS 800 prescribes no high-shear reduction formula for semi-compact sections \(\implies\) allowable reduction = 0%.

6. Final Answer:

Maximum reduction = Zero | Correct option: (A)

questions.question: In the reinforced beam section shown in the figure (not drawn to scale), the nominal cover provided at the bottom of the beam as per IS 456-2000, is
questions.explanation:
Reinforced Concrete Structures | Detailing of Beams

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Comprehension / Application
  • Given Data:
    • Distance from bottom concrete face to centroid of main reinforcement = 50 mm
    • Main tension reinforcement: 3 bars of 16 mm diameter (\(\phi_{main} = 16\) mm)
    • Stirrups: 2-legged, 12 mm diameter @ 90 mm c/c (\(\phi_{stirrup} = 12\) mm)
  • Aim: Calculate the nominal cover provided at the bottom of the beam.

3. Core Concepts:

  • Nominal Cover (IS 456:2000, Clause 26.4.1): Distance from the extreme outer concrete surface to the outermost surface of reinforcing steel (links, stirrups, or main bars — whichever is outermost).
  • Effective Cover: Distance from the extreme outer concrete surface to the centroid of the main tension reinforcement.

4. Solution Method:

  1. Determine the effective cover from the given data.
  2. Subtract the radius of the main bar to find the clear distance to the bottom of the main bar.
  3. Subtract the stirrup diameter (since stirrup wraps around main bar) to find the clear cover to outermost steel.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Effective Cover \((d_{eff}) = 50\) mm
  2. Radius of main bar: \(r_{main} = \dfrac{16}{2} = 8\) mm
  3. Distance from bottom face to bottommost edge of main bar:\[C_{main} = d_{eff} - r_{main} = 50 - 8 = 42\text{ mm} \]
  4. The stirrup encloses the main bars and sits between them and the bottom concrete face. Outer dimension of stirrup \(= \phi_{stirrup} = 12\) mm.
  5. Nominal Cover:\[C_{nom} = C_{main} - \phi_{stirrup} = 42 - 12 = 30\text{ mm} \]

6. Final Answer:

Nominal Cover \(= 30\) mm | Correct option: (A)

questions.question: The coefficient of average rolling friction of a road is \( f_r \) and its grade is +G%. If the grade of this road is doubled, what will be the percentage change in the braking distance (for the design vehicle to come to a stop) measured along the horizontal (assume all other parameters are kept unchanged)?
questions.explanation:
Highway Engineering | Geometric Design

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Analysis
  • Given Data:
    • Coefficient of average rolling friction \(= f_r\)
    • Initial grade \(= +G\%\)
    • Final grade \(= +2G\%\) (doubled)
  • Aim: Determine the percentage change in the horizontal braking distance.

3. Core Concepts:

  • Braking Distance (\(L\)): On a gradient \(n\), the effective deceleration is modified by gravity along the slope:\[L = \dfrac{v^2}{2g_{acc}(f_r \pm n)} \]where \(n = G/100 = 0.01G\) in decimal format.
  • Percentage Change: \(\dfrac{L_{final} - L_{initial}}{L_{initial}} \times 100\)

4. Solution Method:

Formulate braking distances for both grades, find their algebraic difference, divide by the initial braking distance, and express as a percentage magnitude.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Initial braking distance (\(L_1\)):\[L_1 = \dfrac{v^2}{2g_{acc}(f_r + 0.01G)} \]
  2. Final braking distance (\(L_2\)) with doubled grade:\[L_2 = \dfrac{v^2}{2g_{acc}(f_r + 0.02G)} \]
  3. Change in braking distance (\(\Delta L = L_2 - L_1\)):\[ \Delta L = \dfrac{v^2}{2g_{acc}} \left[\dfrac{(f_r + 0.01G) - (f_r + 0.02G)}{(f_r + 0.02G)(f_r + 0.01G)} \right] = \dfrac{v^2}{2g_{acc}} \cdot \dfrac{-0.01G}{(f_r + 0.02G)(f_r + 0.01G)} \]
  4. Percentage change:\[\%\text{ Change} = \dfrac{\Delta L}{L_1} \times 100 = \dfrac{-0.01G}{(f_r + 0.02G)(f_r + 0.01G)} \times (f_r + 0.01G) \times 100 = \dfrac{-0.01G}{f_r + 0.02G} \times 100 \]

The absolute magnitude of the percentage decrease is:

\[\dfrac{0.01G}{f_r + 0.02G} \times 100 \]

6. Final Answer:

\(\%\text{ Change} = \dfrac{0.01G}{f_r + 0.02G} \times 100\) | Correct option: (A)

The temperature of the top and bottom fibre of the slab are \( T_t \) and \( T_b \), respectively. Given: the coefficient of thermal expansion = \( \alpha \) and the elastic modulus = \( E \).     • Base condition: Frictionless
    • Temperature gradient: \(T_t > T_b\)
    • Concrete unit weight: Zero
  • Aim: Calculate the maximum thermal stress.

3. Core Concepts:

  • Thermal stresses develop strictly due to restraint of natural temperature-induced volumetric changes.
  • Frictional (Longitudinal) Stress: Due to subgrade friction resisting uniform expansion/contraction.
  • Warping Stress: Due to temperature gradient causing the slab to curl. The slab's self-weight acts as downward restraint against curling, generating internal bending stresses.

4. Solution Method:

Check the constraints provided by the problem boundary conditions to see if any restraint exists.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Analyze Frictional Restraint: Base is frictionless (\(f = 0\)). The slab expands or contracts horizontally without any resistance.\[\sigma_{friction} = 0 \]
  2. Analyze Warping Restraint: A temperature gradient (\(T_t > T_b\)) causes the slab to curl upwards. However, the unit weight of concrete is assumed to be zero.
  3. With zero self-weight, there is no downward force restraining curling motion. The slab undergoes completely unrestrained geometric warping — no internal stresses are generated.\[\sigma_{warping} = 0 \]
  4. Total maximum thermal stress \(= 0 + 0 = 0\).

6. Final Answer:

Maximum thermal stress = Zero | Correct option: (D)

questions.explanation:

  • Taxonomy: Comprehension
  • Given Data:
    • Channel section: Rectangular
    • Flow state: Critical flow
  • Aim: Find the ratio of the velocity head to the flow depth.

3. Core Concepts:

  • Critical Flow Condition: Specific energy is minimum; Froude Number \((Fr) = 1\).
  • Froude Number for rectangular channel: \(Fr = \dfrac{V}{\sqrt{gy}}\)
  • Velocity Head: \(H_v = \dfrac{V^2}{2g}\)

4. Solution Method:

Express critical velocity \(V_c\) in terms of critical depth \(y_c\) using \(Fr = 1\), then substitute into the velocity head equation and divide by \(y_c\).

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. For critical flow: \(\dfrac{V_c}{\sqrt{g y_c}} = 1\)
  2. Squaring: \(V_c^2 = g y_c\)
  3. Velocity head: \(H_v = \dfrac{V_c^2}{2g} = \dfrac{g y_c}{2g} = \dfrac{y_c}{2}\)
  4. Required ratio:\[\dfrac{H_v}{y_c} = \dfrac{y_c/2}{y_c} = \dfrac{1}{2} \]

6. Final Answer:

Ratio of velocity head to flow depth \(= \dfrac{1}{2}\) | Correct option: (A)

    • Estimation methods: Arithmetic Mean (\(P_A\)) and Thiessen Polygon (\(P_T\))
  • Aim: Determine the relationship between \(P_A\) and \(P_T\).

3. Core Concepts:

  • Arithmetic Mean Method (\(P_A\)): Straight average — each gauge has equal weight (\(1/3\)).\[P_A = \dfrac{P_1 + P_2 + P_3}{3} \]
  • Thiessen Polygon Method (\(P_T\)): Area-weighted average — each gauge's influence depends on its polygon area \(A_i\).\[P_T = \dfrac{A_1 P_1 + A_2 P_2 + A_3 P_3}{A_{total}} \]

4. Solution Method:

Evaluate whether independent variables (rainfall depth \(P_i\) and geographical placement \(A_i\)) force a specific mathematical inequality.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Gauges are at arbitrary locations \(\implies\) unequal polygon areas (\(A_1 \neq A_2 \neq A_3\)).
  2. Arithmetic mean rigidly assigns weight \(1/3\) to each gauge regardless of spatial coverage.
  3. Thiessen method dynamically assigns weights \(A_i/A\).
  4. If a gauge with high rainfall covers a small polygon (\(A_i/A < 1/3\)), \(P_A\) over-weights it \(\implies P_A > P_T\).
  5. Conversely, if a gauge with high rainfall covers a dominant polygon (\(A_i/A > 1/3\)), \(P_T\) over-weights it \(\implies P_A < P_T\).
  6. Since rainfall depths and arbitrary areas are independent random variables, neither method intrinsically overestimates the other in all conditions.

6. Final Answer:

There is no definite relationship between \(P_A\) and \(P_T\) | Correct option: (D)

3. Core Concepts:

  • Rankine's Earth Pressure Theory: For a smooth, vertical wall retaining cohesionless backfill inclined at angle \(\beta\), the active earth pressure acts parallel to the slope of the backfill (i.e., at angle \(\beta\) with the horizontal).
  • Hydrostatic Pressure Distribution: \(p_a = K_a \gamma z \cos\beta\) — pressure increases linearly with depth, forming a triangular distribution.
  • Resultant Thrust Application Point: \(P_a\) acts through the centroid of the triangular distribution, at a height of \(H/3\) from the base.

4. Solution Method:

  1. Identify the point of application from the geometry of the pressure distribution.
  2. Identify the direction of the resultant thrust from Rankine's theory for inclined backfills.
  3. Match with the given options.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Pressure distribution shape: Linear (Triangular), since \(p_a \propto z\).
  2. Centroid height from base: For a triangle of height \(H\), the centroid is at \(H/3\) from the base.
    \(\therefore P_a\) acts at height \(H/3\) from the base of the wall.
  3. Direction of pressure: By Rankine's conjugate stress assumptions, the lateral pressure on a vertical plane parallel to an inclined ground surface is parallel to that surface.
    \(\therefore\) The thrust acts at angle \(\beta\) with the horizontal.

6. Final Answer:

\(P_a\) acts at height \(H/3\) from the base and at angle \(\beta\) with the horizontal | Correct option: (C)

questions.title: GATE CE 2019 Set 1 | CE Q17
questions.subject: Geotechnical Engineering (Soil)
questions.question: In a soil specimen, the total stress, effective stress, hydraulic gradient and critical hydraulic gradient are \( \sigma \), \( \sigma' \), \( i \) and \( i_c \), respectively. For initiation of quicksand condition, which one of the following statements is TRUE?
questions.explanation:
Geotechnical Engineering | Permeability and Seepage

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Comprehension
  • Given Data:
    • Total stress \(= \sigma\), Effective stress \(= \sigma'\)
    • Hydraulic gradient \(= i\), Critical hydraulic gradient \(= i_c\)
  • Aim: Identify the true condition of stresses and gradients at the initiation of the quicksand condition.

3. Core Concepts:

  • Effective Stress Principle: \(\sigma' = \sigma - u\)
  • Seepage Force: Upward seepage increases pore water pressure \((u)\), thereby reducing effective stress between soil grains.
  • Quicksand Condition: A hydraulic condition (not a soil type) in cohesionless soils when upward seepage pressure equals buoyant unit weight of soil — inter-granular contact is lost and soil loses all shear strength.
  • Critical Hydraulic Gradient (\(i_c\)): The gradient at which effective stress exactly becomes zero (\(\sigma' = 0\)).

4. Solution Method:

  1. Apply the mechanical definition of quicksand to the shear strength formula.
  2. Deduce values of \(\sigma'\) and \(i\) at this critical state.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Shear strength (Mohr-Coulomb): \(\tau = c' + \sigma'\tan\phi'\)
  2. For cohesionless sand (\(c' = 0\)): \(\tau = \sigma'\tan\phi'\)
  3. Under quicksand, soil behaves like a liquid: \(\tau = 0 \implies \sigma' = 0\).
  4. The upward gradient required to nullify effective stress is precisely the critical hydraulic gradient: \(i = i_c\).
  5. The total stress \(\sigma\) does not become zero — only effective stress is offset by pore water pressure.

6. Final Answer:

\(\sigma' = 0\) and \(i = i_c\) | Correct option: (B)

questions.title: GATE CE 2019 Set 1 | CE Q19
questions.subject: Structural Analysis & Mechanics
questions.question: For a given loading on a rectangular plain concrete beam with an overall depth of 500 mm, the compressive strain and tensile strain developed at the extreme fibers are of the same magnitude of \( 2.5 \times 10^{-4} \). The curvature in the beam cross-section (in \( m^{-1} \), round off to 3 decimal places), is ________
questions.explanation:
Structural Engineering | Solid Mechanics

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Rectangular plain concrete beam, overall depth \(D = 500\) mm \(= 0.5\) m
    • Compressive strain at extreme top fiber: \(\varepsilon_c = 2.5 \times 10^{-4}\)
    • Tensile strain at extreme bottom fiber: \(\varepsilon_t = 2.5 \times 10^{-4}\) (magnitude)
  • Aim: Calculate the curvature in m\(^{-1}\).

3. Core Concepts:

  • Euler-Bernoulli Beam Theory: Plane cross-sections remain plane — linear strain distribution across depth.
  • Curvature (\(\kappa\)): \(\kappa = \dfrac{1}{R} = \dfrac{\varepsilon}{y}\), where \(y\) is the distance from the neutral axis.
  • Neutral Axis Location: Since \(\varepsilon_c = \varepsilon_t\), the neutral axis lies at mid-depth.

4. Solution Method:

  1. Locate the neutral axis using strain compatibility.
  2. Determine \(y\) from the neutral axis to the extreme fiber.
  3. Apply \(\kappa = \varepsilon / y\) and convert to m\(^{-1}\).

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Since \(\varepsilon_c = \varepsilon_t\), neutral axis is at mid-depth:\[y_c = \dfrac{D}{2} = \dfrac{0.5}{2} = 0.25\text{ m} \]
  2. Calculate curvature:\[\kappa = \dfrac{\varepsilon_c}{y_c} = \dfrac{2.5 \times 10^{-4}}{0.25} = 10 \times 10^{-4} = 0.001\text{ m}^{-1} \]

6. Final Answer:

Curvature \(\kappa = 0.001\) m\(^{-1}\) | Accepted key range: 0.001 to 0.001

questions.title: GATE CE 2019 Set 1 | CE Q20
questions.subject: Environmental Engineering
questions.question: A completely mixed dilute suspension of sand particles having diameters 0.25, 0.35, 0.40, 0.45 and 0.50 mm are filled in a transparent glass column of diameter 10 cm and height 2.50 m. The suspension is allowed to settle without any disturbance. It is observed that all particles of diameter 0.35 mm settle to the bottom of the column in 30 s. For the same period of 30 s, the percentage removal (round off to integer value) of particles of diameters 0.45 and 0.50 mm from the suspension is ________
questions.explanation:
Environmental Engineering | Water Treatment (Sedimentation)

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Analysis
  • Given Data:
    • Completely mixed dilute sand suspension with particle diameters: 0.25, 0.35, 0.40, 0.45, 0.50 mm
    • Column diameter \(= 10\) cm, Settling depth \(H = 2.50\) m
    • 100% of 0.35 mm particles settle to the bottom in \(t = 30\) s
  • Aim: Determine percentage removal of 0.45 mm and 0.50 mm particles in 30 s.

3. Core Concepts:

  • Discrete Particle Settling (Type I): Settling velocity \(v_s\) strictly increases with particle diameter \(d\). Larger particles settle faster.
  • Critical Settling Velocity (\(v_c\)): \(v_c = H/t\). Any particle with \(v_s \ge v_c\) is 100% removed.
  • Removal Efficiency: All particles with diameter \(d > d_c\) are completely removed (100%) since their \(v_s > v_c\).

4. Solution Method:

  1. Evaluate the critical settling condition given by the 0.35 mm particle.
  2. Compare target particle diameters (0.45 mm and 0.50 mm) to the critical diameter.
  3. Deduce removal efficiency directly from settling velocity characteristics.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Critical condition: 0.35 mm particles achieve 100% removal in 30 s:\[v_c = \dfrac{2.50\text{ m}}{30\text{ s}} \approx 0.0833\text{ m/s} \]
  2. \(d_{0.45} = 0.45\text{ mm} > 0.35\text{ mm} \implies v_{s(0.45)} > v_c\)
  3. \(d_{0.50} = 0.50\text{ mm} > 0.35\text{ mm} \implies v_{s(0.50)} > v_c\)
  4. Both particles travel distance \(H\) in less than 30 s \(\implies\) 100% removal at the 30 s mark.

6. Final Answer:

Removal of 0.45 mm and 0.50 mm particles \(= 100\%\) | Accepted key range: 100 to 100

questions.title: GATE CE 2019 Set 1 | CE Q21

questions.question: The maximum number of vehicles observed in any five minute period during the peak hour is 160. If the total flow in the peak hour is 1000 vehicles, the five minute peak hour factor (round off to 2 decimal places) is ________
questions.explanation:
Transportation Engineering | Traffic Engineering

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Maximum vehicle volume in any 5-minute period, \(V_{5(\max)} = 160\) vehicles
    • Total overall volume in peak hour, \(V = 1000\) vehicles
    • Sub-interval duration, \(n = 5\) minutes
  • Aim: Calculate the 5-minute Peak Hour Factor (\(\text{PHF}_5\)), rounded to 2 decimal places.

3. Core Concepts:

  • Peak Hour Factor (PHF): Quantifies traffic volume fluctuation within the peak hour.\[\text{PHF}_n = \dfrac{\text{Total Hourly Volume}}{N \times \text{Maximum }n\text{-minute Volume}} \]where \(N = 60/n\) is the number of \(n\)-minute sub-intervals per hour.

4. Solution Method:

  1. Determine the number of 5-minute intervals in one hour (\(N\)).
  2. Compute the theoretical maximum hourly flow rate.
  3. Divide actual total volume by this theoretical maximum.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Number of intervals: \(N = 60/5 = 12\)
  2. Theoretical maximum hourly flow: \(12 \times 160 = 1920\) veh/hr
  3. \(\text{PHF}_5 = \dfrac{1000}{1920} = 0.52083 \approx 0.52\)

6. Final Answer:

\(\text{PHF}_5 = 0.52\) | Accepted key range: 0.51 to 0.53

questions.title: GATE CE 2019 Set 1 | CE Q22
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question:
A circular duct carrying water gradually contracts from a diameter of 30 cm to 15 cm. The figure (not drawn to scale) shows the arrangement of differential manometer attached to the duct.

When the water flows, the differential manometer shows a deflection of 8 cm of mercury (Hg). The values of specific gravity of mercury and water are 13.6 and 1.0, respectively. Consider the acceleration due to gravity, \( g = 9.81\ m/s^2 \). Assuming frictionless flow, the flow rate (in \( m^3/s \), round off to 3 decimal places) through the duct is ________
questions.explanation:
Fluid Mechanics | Fluid Dynamics (Venturimeter)

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Upstream diameter \(D_1 = 30\) cm \(= 0.3\) m; Contracted diameter \(D_2 = 15\) cm \(= 0.15\) m
    • Manometer reading \(x = 8\) cm \(= 0.08\) m; \(S_m = 13.6\), \(S_w = 1.0\)
    • \(g = 9.81\) m/s\(^2\); Frictionless flow \(\implies C_d = 1.0\)
  • Aim: Find volumetric flow rate \(Q\) in m\(^3\)/s (3 decimal places).

3. Core Concepts:

  • Continuity Equation: \(Q = A_1 V_1 = A_2 V_2\)
  • Bernoulli's Equation (horizontal): \(h = \dfrac{P_1 - P_2}{\gamma_w} = \dfrac{V_2^2 - V_1^2}{2g}\)
  • Manometry: \(h = x\left(\dfrac{S_m}{S_w} - 1\right)\)
  • Discharge Formula: \(Q = C_d\dfrac{A_1 A_2 \sqrt{2gh}}{\sqrt{A_1^2 - A_2^2}}\)

4. Solution Method:

  1. Compute cross-sectional areas \(A_1\) and \(A_2\).
  2. Compute differential pressure head \(h\) from manometer reading.
  3. Input values into the discharge equation.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Areas:\[A_1 = \dfrac{\pi}{4}(0.3)^2 = 0.070686\text{ m}^2, \quad A_2 = \dfrac{\pi}{4}(0.15)^2 = 0.017671\text{ m}^2 \]
  2. Differential Head:\[h = 0.08 \times (13.6 - 1) = 0.08 \times 12.6 = 1.008\text{ m of water} \]
  3. Denominator term:\[\sqrt{A_1^2 - A_2^2} = \sqrt{(0.070686)^2 - (0.017671)^2} = 0.068436\text{ m}^2 \]
  4. Velocity factor:\[\sqrt{2 \times 9.81 \times 1.008} = \sqrt{19.777} = 4.4471\text{ m/s} \]
  5. Flow rate:\[Q = 1.0 \times \dfrac{0.070686 \times 0.017671}{0.068436} \times 4.4471 = 0.018250 \times 4.4471 \approx 0.081\text{ m}^3/\text{s} \]

6. Final Answer:

\(Q = 0.081\) m\(^3\)/s | Accepted key range: 0.078 to 0.085

questions.title: GATE CE 2019 Set 1 | CE Q23
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question: The probability that the annual maximum flood discharge will exceed 25000 \( m^3/s \), at least once in next 5 years is found to be 0.25. The return period of this flood event (in years, round off to 1 decimal place) is ________
questions.explanation:
Hydrology | Floods / Probability

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Annual maximum flood discharge \(> 25000\) m\(^3\)/s
    • Probability of event occurring at least once (Risk, \(R\)) \(= 0.25\)
    • Time span \((n) = 5\) years
  • Aim: Calculate the return period \(T\) in years (rounded to 1 decimal place).

3. Core Concepts:

  • Return Period (\(T\)): Statistical average time between occurrences of a given event.
  • Annual Exceedance Probability: \(p = 1/T\)
  • Hydrological Risk (\(R\)):\[R = 1 - \left(1 - \dfrac{1}{T}\right)^n \]

4. Solution Method:

  1. Substitute known \(R\) and \(n\) into the risk equation.
  2. Isolate and solve for \(\left(1 - 1/T\right)\).
  3. Take the reciprocal to find \(T\).

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Substitute knowns:\[0.25 = 1 - \left(1 - \dfrac{1}{T}\right)^5 \]
  2. Rearrange:\[\left(1 - \dfrac{1}{T}\right)^5 = 0.75 \]
  3. Take the 5th root:\[1 - \dfrac{1}{T} = (0.75)^{0.2} \approx 0.94409 \]
  4. Solve for \(p\):\[\dfrac{1}{T} = 1 - 0.94409 = 0.05591 \]
  5. Return period:\[T = \dfrac{1}{0.05591} \approx 17.9\text{ years} \]

6. Final Answer:

Return Period \(T = 17.9\) years | Accepted key range: 17.8 to 18.0

questions.title: GATE CE 2019 Set 1 | CE Q24
questions.subject: Geotechnical Engineering (Soil)
questions.question: A soil has specific gravity of its solids equal to 2.65. The mass density of water is 1000 \( kg/m^3 \). Considering zero air voids and 10% moisture content of the soil sample, the dry density (in \( kg/m^3 \), round off to 1 decimal place) would be ________
questions.explanation:
Geotechnical Engineering | Soil Properties

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Specific gravity of soil solids \(G = 2.65\)
    • Mass density of water \(\rho_w = 1000\) kg/m\(^3\)
    • Air void percentage \(= 0\) (Zero air voids \(\implies S = 100\%\))
    • Moisture content \(w = 10\% = 0.10\)
  • Aim: Calculate the theoretical dry density \(\rho_d\) in kg/m\(^3\) (to 1 decimal place).

3. Core Concepts:

  • Zero Air Voids: All voids are filled with water \(\implies S = 1\).
  • Phase Relationship: \(S \cdot e = w \cdot G\)
  • Dry Density: \(\rho_d = \dfrac{G\rho_w}{1+e}\)
  • Substituting \(e = wG\) (from \(S=1\)):\[\rho_{d(\max)} = \dfrac{G\rho_w}{1 + wG} \]

4. Solution Method:

  1. Apply \(S \cdot e = w \cdot G\) with \(S=1\) to calculate \(e\).
  2. Substitute into the dry density formula.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Find void ratio (\(e\)):\[1 \times e = 0.10 \times 2.65 \implies e = 0.265 \]
  2. Calculate dry density:\[\rho_d = \dfrac{2.65 \times 1000}{1 + 0.265} = \dfrac{2650}{1.265} = 2094.9\text{ kg/m}^3 \]

6. Final Answer:

\(\rho_d = 2094.9\) kg/m\(^3\) | Accepted key range: 2086.6 to 2095.0

questions.title: GATE CE 2019 Set 1 | CE Q25
questions.subject: Geotechnical Engineering (Soil)
questions.question: A concentrated load of 500 kN is applied on an elastic half space. The ratio of the increase in vertical normal stress at depths of 2 m and 4 m along the point of the loading, as per Boussinesq's theory, would be ________
questions.explanation:
Geotechnical Engineering | Stresses in Soil (Boussinesq's Theory)

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Concentrated surface load \(Q = 500\) kN
    • Depth 1: \(z_1 = 2\) m; Depth 2: \(z_2 = 4\) m
    • Both points lie on the vertical axis directly beneath the load (\(r = 0\))
  • Aim: Compute the ratio \(\dfrac{\sigma_{z1}}{\sigma_{z2}}\).

3. Core Concepts:

  • Boussinesq's General Equation:\[ \sigma_z = \dfrac{3Q}{2\pi z^2} \left[\dfrac{1}{1 + (r/z)^2} \right]^{5/2} \]
  • Simplified for central axis (\(r = 0\)):\[\sigma_z = \dfrac{3Q}{2\pi z^2} \]
  • Proportionality: Directly below a point load: \(\sigma_z \propto \dfrac{1}{z^2}\)

4. Solution Method:

  1. Use the \(1/z^2\) proportionality — note that \(Q\) cancels out in the ratio.
  2. Substitute depths to find the integer ratio.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

\[\sigma_{z1} \propto \dfrac{1}{z_1^2} = \dfrac{1}{2^2} = \dfrac{1}{4} \]\[\sigma_{z2} \propto \dfrac{1}{z_2^2} = \dfrac{1}{4^2} = \dfrac{1}{16} \]\[\dfrac{\sigma_{z1}}{\sigma_{z2}} = \dfrac{1/4}{1/16} = \dfrac{16}{4} = 4 \]

6. Final Answer:

\(\dfrac{\sigma_{z1}}{\sigma_{z2}} = 4\) | Accepted key range: 4 to 4

questions.title: GATE CE 2019 Set 1 | CE Q26
questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.question: Which one of the following is NOT a correct statement?
options: The function \( \sqrt[x]{x} \), (\( x > 0 \)), has the global maxima at \( x = e \)
The function \( \sqrt[x]{x} \), (\( x > 0 \)), has the global minima at \( x = e \)
The function \( x^3 \) has neither global minima nor global maxima
The function \( |x| \) has the global minima at \( x = 0 \)

structuredOptions.label: A
structuredOptions.text: The function \( \sqrt[x]{x} \), (\( x > 0 \)), has the global maxima at \( x = e \)
structuredOptions.html: The function \( \sqrt[x]{x} \), (\( x > 0 \)), has the global maxima at \( x = e \)

structuredOptions.label: B
structuredOptions.text: The function \( \sqrt[x]{x} \), (\( x > 0 \)), has the global minima at \( x = e \)
structuredOptions.html: The function \( \sqrt[x]{x} \), (\( x > 0 \)), has the global minima at \( x = e \)

structuredOptions.label: C
structuredOptions.text: The function \( x^3 \) has neither global minima nor global maxima
structuredOptions.html: The function \( x^3 \) has neither global minima nor global maxima

structuredOptions.label: D
structuredOptions.text: The function \( |x| \) has the global minima at \( x = 0 \)
structuredOptions.html: The function \( |x| \) has the global minima at \( x = 0 \)

questions.explanation:
Engineering Mathematics | Calculus

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application / Analysis
  • Given Data: Four statements defining mathematical functions and claiming their global extrema (maxima/minima).
  • Aim: To identify which of the four statements is NOT correct.

3. Core Concepts:

A function \(f(x)\) has a local extremum where its first derivative \(f'(x) = 0\) or is undefined.

To find the extrema of functions with variable bases and exponents, like \(f(x) = x^{1/x}\), we use logarithmic differentiation.

The nature of the extremum (global maximum vs. global minimum) is evaluated by checking the sign change of the first derivative around the critical point or assessing limits at domain boundaries.

4. Solution Method:

Analyze the statements one by one:

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

Statements (A) & (B): \(f(x) = \sqrt[x]{x} = x^{1/x}\) for \(x > 0\)

Let \(y = x^{1/x}\). Taking the natural logarithm on both sides:

\[\ln y = \dfrac{1}{x} \ln x \]

Differentiating both sides with respect to \(x\):

\[\dfrac{1}{y} \dfrac{dy}{dx} = \left( -\dfrac{1}{x^2} \right) \ln x + \dfrac{1}{x} \left( \dfrac{1}{x} \right) \]\[\dfrac{dy}{dx} = y \left( \dfrac{1 - \ln x}{x^2} \right) = x^{1/x} \left( \dfrac{1 - \ln x}{x^2} \right) \]

To find the critical point, set \(f'(x) = 0\):

\[1 - \ln x = 0 \implies \ln x = 1 \implies x = e \]
  • For \(x \in (0, e)\), \(1 - \ln x > 0 \implies f'(x) > 0\) (Function is increasing)
  • For \(x \in (e, \infty)\), \(1 - \ln x < 0 \implies f'(x) < 0\) (Function is decreasing)

Because the function increases up to \(x = e\) and strictly decreases thereafter, it possesses a global maximum at \(x = e\).

  • Statement (A) says it has a global maximum at \(x = e\) → TRUE
  • Statement (B) says it has a global minimum at \(x = e\) → FALSE

Statement (C): \(f(x) = x^3\)

The domain is \(\mathbb{R}\). As \(x \to \infty,\ f(x) \to \infty\) and as \(x \to -\infty,\ f(x) \to -\infty\). It continuously increases since \(f'(x) = 3x^2 \ge 0\). Hence, it has neither a global maximum nor a global minimum → TRUE.

Statement (D): \(f(x) = |x|\)

The absolute value function is strictly non-negative (\(|x| \ge 0\)). At \(x = 0\), \(f(0) = 0\). Hence, it has a global minimum at \(x = 0\) → TRUE.

6. Final Answer:

Statement (B) is the incorrect statement. | Correct option: (B)

questions.title: GATE CE 2019 Set 1 | CE Q27
questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.question: A one-dimensional domain is discretized into \( N \) sub-domains of width \( \Delta x \) with node numbers \( i = 0, 1, 2, 3, ..., N \). If the time scale is discretized in steps of \( \Delta t \), the forward-time and centered-space finite difference approximation at \( i^{th} \) node and \( n^{th} \) time step, for the partial differential equation \( \dfrac{\partial v}{\partial t} = \beta \dfrac{\partial^2 v}{\partial x^2} \) is
questions.explanation:
Engineering Mathematics | Numerical Methods

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Recall / Comprehension
  • Given Data: The 1-D partial differential equation (PDE): \(\dfrac{\partial v}{\partial t} = \beta \dfrac{\partial^2 v}{\partial x^2}\)
  • Aim: To construct the finite difference approximation using a forward-time and centered-space (FTCS) scheme at node \(i\) and time step \(n\).

3. Core Concepts:

Forward-Time Difference (First Order):

\[\dfrac{\partial v}{\partial t} \approx \dfrac{v_i^{(n+1)} - v_i^{(n)}}{\Delta t} \]

Centered-Space Difference (Second Order):

\[\dfrac{\partial^2 v}{\partial x^2} \approx \dfrac{v_{i+1}^{(n)} - 2v_i^{(n)} + v_{i-1}^{(n)}}{(\Delta x)^2} \]

4. Solution Method & Execution:

Substituting these standard finite difference approximations directly into the governing PDE:

\[ \dfrac{v_i^{(n+1)} - v_i^{(n)}}{\Delta t} = \beta \left[\dfrac{v_{i+1}^{(n)} - 2v_i^{(n)} + v_{i-1}^{(n)}}{(\Delta x)^2} \right] \]

This matches the formulation provided in Option (A).

Note: Option C utilizes backward-time, Option D utilizes centered-time, and Option B is structurally invalid.

5. Final Answer:

The valid FTCS scheme formula. | Correct option: (A)

questions.title: GATE CE 2019 Set 1 | CE Q28
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question: A rectangular open channel has a width of 5 m and a bed slope of 0.001. For a uniform flow of depth 2 m, the velocity is 2 m/s. The Manning’s roughness coefficient for the channel is
questions.explanation:
Fluid Mechanics & Hydraulics | Open Channel Flow

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Width \((B) = 5\) m
    • Flow depth \((y) = 2\) m
    • Velocity \((V) = 2\) m/s
    • Bed slope \((S_0) = 0.001\)
  • Aim: To determine the Manning's roughness coefficient \((n)\).

3. Core Concepts:

Manning's Equation for Uniform Flow:

\[V = \dfrac{1}{n} R^{2/3} S_0^{1/2} \]

Hydraulic Radius \((R)\): \(R = \dfrac{A}{P}\), where \(A\) is the cross-sectional area and \(P\) is the wetted perimeter.

4. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Compute Cross-sectional Area \((A)\) and Wetted Perimeter \((P)\):
    \[A = B \times y = 5 \text{ m} \times 2 \text{ m} = 10 \text{ m}^2 \]\[P = B + 2y = 5 \text{ m} + 2(2 \text{ m}) = 9 \text{ m} \]
  2. Compute Hydraulic Radius \((R)\):
    \[R = \dfrac{A}{P} = \dfrac{10}{9} \approx 1.1111 \text{ m} \]
  3. Rearrange Manning's formula and solve for \(n\):
    \[n = \dfrac{R^{2/3} S_0^{1/2}}{V} \]\[n = \dfrac{(10/9)^{2/3} \times (0.001)^{1/2}}{2} \]\[n = \dfrac{1.07276 \times 0.03162}{2} = \dfrac{0.03392}{2} = 0.01696 \]
    Rounding off to three decimal places gives \(n \approx 0.017\).

5. Final Answer:

\(n = 0.017\) | Correct option: (B)

questions.title: GATE CE 2019 Set 1 | CE Q30
questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.question: Consider two functions: \( x = \psi \ln \phi \) and \( y = \phi \ln \psi \). Which one of the following is the correct expression for \( \dfrac{\partial \psi}{\partial x} \)?
questions.explanation:
Engineering Mathematics | Calculus

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data: Two coupled implicit functions: \(x = \psi \ln \phi\) and \(y = \phi \ln \psi\)
  • Aim: Extract the partial derivative \(\dfrac{\partial \psi}{\partial x}\).

3. Core Concepts:

To find \(\dfrac{\partial \psi}{\partial x}\), we treat \(x\) as the independent variable and look for how \(\psi\) changes, while keeping \(y\) strictly constant (which means \(dy = 0\)). We utilize the concept of implicit differentiation via total differentials.

4. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Take the total differential of both equations:
    \[dx = (\ln \phi)\, d\psi + \left( \psi \cdot \dfrac{1}{\phi} \right) d\phi \quad \cdots \text{(Eq. 1)} \]\[dy = (\ln \psi)\, d\phi + \left( \phi \cdot \dfrac{1}{\psi} \right) d\psi \quad \cdots \text{(Eq. 2)} \]
  2. Apply the partial derivative condition (\(\dfrac{\partial}{\partial x}\) holds \(y\) constant, so \(dy = 0\)) in Eq. 2:
    \[0 = (\ln \psi)\, d\phi + \left( \dfrac{\phi}{\psi} \right) d\psi \]
    Express \(d\phi\) in terms of \(d\psi\):
    \[d\phi = - \left( \dfrac{\phi}{\psi \ln \psi} \right) d\psi \]
  3. Substitute \(d\phi\) into Eq. 1:
    \[ dx = (\ln \phi)\, d\psi + \dfrac{\psi}{\phi} \left[- \left( \dfrac{\phi}{\psi \ln \psi} \right) d\psi \right] \]\[dx = \left( \ln \phi - \dfrac{1}{\ln \psi} \right) d\psi \]\[dx = \left( \dfrac{\ln \phi \ln \psi - 1}{\ln \psi} \right) d\psi \]
  4. Rearrange to isolate the required derivative:
    \[\dfrac{\partial \psi}{\partial x} = \dfrac{d\psi}{dx} = \dfrac{\ln \psi}{\ln \phi \ln \psi - 1} \]

5. Final Answer:

\(\dfrac{\partial \psi}{\partial x} = \dfrac{\ln \psi}{\ln \phi \ln \psi - 1}\) | Correct option: (D)

questions.title: GATE CE 2019 Set 1 | CE Q31

questions.question: The cross-section of a built-up wooden beam as shown in the figure (not drawn to scale) is subjected to a vertical shear force of 8 kN. The beam is symmetrical about the neutral axis (N.A.) shown, and the moment of inertia about N.A. is \( 1.5 \times 10^9\ mm^4 \). Considering that the nails at the location P are spaced longitudinally (along the length of the beam) at 60 mm, each of the nails at P will be subjected to the shear force of
questions.explanation:
Structural Engineering | Solid Mechanics

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application / Analysis
  • Given Data:
    • Shear force \((V) = 8\) kN \(= 8000\) N
    • Moment of Inertia \((I) = 1.5 \times 10^9\) mm\(^4\)
    • Longitudinal nail spacing \((s) = 60\) mm
    • Symmetrical built-up section of total depth \(= 400\) mm
  • Aim: Calculate the shear force sustained by a single nail at location P.

3. Core Concepts:

Shear Flow Formula: The longitudinal shear force per unit length \((q)\) at an interface is given by:

\[q = \dfrac{VQ}{I} \]

where \(Q\) is the first moment of area of the section being sheared off, taken about the Neutral Axis (N.A.).

Force on Fastener: \(F_{\text{nail}} = q \times s\)

4. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Establish Section Geometry and Locate the Sheared Area:
    The beam is symmetrical, so the Neutral Axis (N.A.) sits at mid-depth (\(200\) mm from the top/bottom).
    Nail "P" holds the bottom-left wooden block against the central web. The area tending to slide longitudinally past the central web is that specific side-block:
    • Block width \((b) = 50\) mm
    • Block depth \((d) = 100\) mm
    • The block's bottom boundary is flush with the beam's overall bottom (\(200\) mm away from the N.A.).
    • Therefore, the block spans from \(y = 100\) mm to \(y = 200\) mm from the N.A.
  2. Calculate Area \((A)\) and Centroid \((\bar{y})\) for the isolated block:
    \[A = 50 \text{ mm} \times 100 \text{ mm} = 5000 \text{ mm}^2 \]
    The centroidal distance \((\bar{y})\) of this rectangular block from the N.A. is:
    \[\bar{y} = 100 \text{ mm} + \dfrac{100 \text{ mm}}{2} = 150 \text{ mm} \]
  3. Calculate First Moment of Area \((Q)\):
    \[Q = A \times \bar{y} = 5000 \text{ mm}^2 \times 150 \text{ mm} = 7.5 \times 10^5 \text{ mm}^3 \]
  4. Calculate Interface Shear Flow \((q)\):
    \[q = \dfrac{VQ}{I} = \dfrac{(8000 \text{ N}) \times (7.5 \times 10^5 \text{ mm}^3)}{1.5 \times 10^9 \text{ mm}^4} \]\[q = \dfrac{6 \times 10^9}{1.5 \times 10^9} = 4 \text{ N/mm} \]
  5. Calculate Force on each nail \((F)\):
    \[F = q \times s = 4 \text{ N/mm} \times 60 \text{ mm} = 240 \text{ N} \]

5. Final Answer:

\(F_{\text{nail}} = 240\) N | Correct option: (C)

questions.title: GATE CE 2019 Set 1 | CE Q32
questions.subject: Structural Analysis & Mechanics
questions.question: The rigid-jointed plane frame QRS shown in the figure is subjected to a load \( P \) at the joint R. Let the axial deformations in the frame be neglected. If the support S undergoes a settlement of \( \Delta = \dfrac{PL^3}{\beta EI} \), the vertical reaction at the support S will become zero when \( \beta \) is equal to
questions.explanation:
Structural Analysis | Indeterminate Structures (Displacement Method)

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application / Analysis
  • Given Data:
    • Rigid-jointed frame QRS with fixed supports at Q and S.
    • Member lengths: \(L_{QR} = L_{RS} = L\)
    • Flexural rigidity: \(EI\) for both members.
    • Axial deformations are negligible.
    • Vertical point load \(P\) acts downwards at joint R.
    • Support S undergoes a downward settlement \(\Delta = \dfrac{PL^3}{\beta EI}\)
    • Vertical reaction at S (\(V_S\)) becomes zero.
  • Aim: Determine the value of the coefficient \(\beta\).

3. Core Concepts:

  • Slope-Deflection Method: Used to relate member end moments to joint displacements and rotations.
  • Kinematic Indeterminacy: Due to negligible axial deformation, the horizontal displacement of R is zero (\(\delta_{Rx} = 0\)), and its vertical displacement matches the settlement of S exactly (\(\delta_{Ry} = \Delta\)).
  • Joint Equilibrium: The sum of moments at a rigid joint must be zero (\(\sum M_R = 0\)). Also, the sum of forces must balance the external load.
  • Sign Convention: Clockwise moments and rotations are positive. Downward translation is considered as a positive relative displacement for calculating fixed-end moments.

4. Solution Method:

  1. Determine the kinematic degrees of freedom at joint R. Since S settles by \(\Delta\) and axial length RS is rigid, R moves down by \(\Delta\).
  2. Write the slope-deflection equations for members QR and RS.
  3. Apply moment equilibrium at joint R to find the unknown joint rotation \(\theta_R\).
  4. Calculate the shear force exerted by member QR on joint R using the member end moments.
  5. Apply vertical equilibrium at joint R. Since \(V_S = 0\), the axial force in RS is zero. Thus, the vertical shear from QR must completely balance the external load \(P\).
  6. Solve for \(\Delta\) in terms of \(P, L, EI\) and extract \(\beta\).

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

Step 1: Kinematics of Joint R

  • Displacement of Q: \(\theta_Q = 0,\ \delta_Q = 0\)
  • Displacement of S: \(\theta_S = 0,\ \delta_{S,\text{vertical}} = \Delta\) (downwards)
  • Displacement of R: \(\theta_R \neq 0,\ \delta_{R,\text{vertical}} = \Delta\) (downwards)
  • Relative transverse displacement for QR: \(\Delta_{QR} = \Delta\) (R goes down relative to Q)
  • Relative transverse displacement for RS: \(\Delta_{RS} = 0\) (both R and S go down by \(\Delta\), so no bending due to sway in RS)

Step 2: Slope-Deflection Equations

For member QR (fixed at Q, settles by \(\Delta\) at R):

\[M_{QR} = \dfrac{2EI}{L} \left(2\theta_Q + \theta_R - \dfrac{3\Delta}{L} \right) = \dfrac{2EI}{L} \theta_R - \dfrac{6EI}{L^2} \Delta \]\[M_{RQ} = \dfrac{2EI}{L} \left(2\theta_R + \theta_Q - \dfrac{3\Delta}{L} \right) = \dfrac{4EI}{L} \theta_R - \dfrac{6EI}{L^2} \Delta \]

For member RS (fixed at S, no relative transverse sway):

\[M_{RS} = \dfrac{2EI}{L} (2\theta_R + \theta_S - 0) = \dfrac{4EI}{L} \theta_R \]

Step 3: Moment Equilibrium at Joint R

\[\sum M_R = 0 \implies M_{RQ} + M_{RS} = 0 \]\[\left( \dfrac{4EI}{L} \theta_R - \dfrac{6EI}{L^2} \Delta \right) + \dfrac{4EI}{L} \theta_R = 0 \]\[\dfrac{8EI}{L} \theta_R = \dfrac{6EI}{L^2} \Delta \implies \theta_R = \dfrac{3\Delta}{4L} \]

Step 4: Shear Force in Member QR

Substitute \(\theta_R\) back into the moments for QR:

\[M_{QR} = \dfrac{2EI}{L} \left(\dfrac{3\Delta}{4L}\right) - \dfrac{6EI}{L^2} \Delta = \dfrac{1.5EI}{L^2} \Delta - \dfrac{6EI}{L^2} \Delta = -4.5 \dfrac{EI}{L^2} \Delta \]\[M_{RQ} = \dfrac{4EI}{L} \left(\dfrac{3\Delta}{4L}\right) - \dfrac{6EI}{L^2} \Delta = \dfrac{3EI}{L^2} \Delta - \dfrac{6EI}{L^2} \Delta = -3 \dfrac{EI}{L^2} \Delta \]

Sum of end moments: \(M_{QR} + M_{RQ} = -7.5\, \dfrac{EI}{L^2} \Delta\) (Counter-clockwise).
To maintain equilibrium, member QR must be subjected to a clockwise shear couple.

\[V_{QR} \times L = 7.5 \dfrac{EI}{L^2} \Delta \implies V_{QR} = 7.5 \dfrac{EI}{L^3} \Delta \]

This shear acts downwards at end R on the member. Therefore, the member pulls upwards on joint R with a force of \(7.5\, \dfrac{EI}{L^3} \Delta\).

Step 5: Vertical Equilibrium at Joint R

The vertical forces acting on joint R are:

  1. External load \(P\) (downwards)
  2. Upward shear from member QR: \(7.5\, \dfrac{EI}{L^3} \Delta\)
  3. Upward axial force from RS: Given as \(V_S = 0\)
\[\sum F_y = 0 \implies 7.5 \dfrac{EI}{L^3} \Delta - P = 0 \implies \Delta = \dfrac{PL^3}{7.5\, EI} \]

Step 6: Determine \(\beta\)

Comparing with the given equation \(\Delta = \dfrac{PL^3}{\beta EI}\), we find \(\beta = 7.5\).

6. Final Answer:

\(\beta = 7.5\) | Correct option: (C)

questions.title: GATE CE 2019 Set 1 | CE Q33
questions.subject: Concrete & Steel Structures

questions.question: If the section shown in the figure turns from fully-elastic to fully-plastic, the depth of neutral axis (N.A.), \( \bar{y} \), decreases by
questions.explanation:
Solid Mechanics | Bending of Beams (Plastic Analysis)

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Comprehension / Application
  • Given Data:
    • T-section with top Flange: \(60\text{ mm} \times 5\text{ mm}\)
    • Web: \(5\text{ mm} \times 60\text{ mm}\)
  • Aim: Determine the decrease in the depth of the neutral axis (\(\bar{y}\)) from the top fiber when the section transitions from fully-elastic to fully-plastic.

3. Core Concepts:

  • Elastic Neutral Axis (E.N.A.): Passes through the centroid of the cross-section.
  • Plastic Neutral Axis (P.N.A.): Divides the total cross-sectional area into two equal halves (Equal Area Axis) under pure bending without axial load.

4. Solution Method:

  1. Calculate the total cross-sectional area.
  2. Find the depth of the E.N.A. by calculating the centroidal distance from the top fiber.
  3. Find the depth of the P.N.A. by locating the axis that bisects the total area.
  4. Subtract the P.N.A. depth from the E.N.A. depth to find the decrease.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

Step 1: Area Calculations

  • Flange Area \((A_1) = 60\text{ mm} \times 5\text{ mm} = 300\text{ mm}^2\)
  • Web Area \((A_2) = 5\text{ mm} \times 60\text{ mm} = 300\text{ mm}^2\)
  • Total Area \((A) = A_1 + A_2 = 600\text{ mm}^2\)

Step 2: Depth of Elastic Neutral Axis (\(\bar{y}_e\))

Taking moments of area about the top edge (\(y = 0\)):

  • Centroid of flange: \(y_1 = 5/2 = 2.5\text{ mm}\)
  • Centroid of web: \(y_2 = 5 + (60/2) = 35\text{ mm}\)
\[\bar{y}_e = \dfrac{A_1 y_1 + A_2 y_2}{A} = \dfrac{(300 \times 2.5) + (300 \times 35)}{600} = \dfrac{750 + 10500}{600} = \dfrac{11250}{600} = 18.75\text{ mm} \]

Step 3: Depth of Plastic Neutral Axis (\(\bar{y}_p\))

The P.N.A. requires the area above to equal the area below: \(A_{\text{top}} = A_{\text{bottom}} = A/2 = 300\text{ mm}^2\).
Notice that the area of the top flange alone is exactly \(300\text{ mm}^2\).
Therefore, the equal area axis lies exactly at the junction of the flange and the web.

\[\bar{y}_p = 5\text{ mm} \]

Step 4: Decrease in Neutral Axis Depth

\[\text{Decrease} = \bar{y}_e - \bar{y}_p = 18.75\text{ mm} - 5\text{ mm} = 13.75\text{ mm} \]

6. Final Answer:

Decrease \(= 13.75\) mm | Correct option: (C)

questions.title: GATE CE 2019 Set 1 | CE Q34
questions.subject: Environmental Engineering
questions.question: Sedimentation basin in a water treatment plant is designed for a flow rate of 0.2 \( m^3/s \). The basin is rectangular with a length of 32 m, width of 8 m, and depth of 4 m. Assume that the settling velocity of these particles is governed by the Stokes’ law. Given: density of the particles = 2.5 g/cm³; density of water = 1 g/cm³; dynamic viscosity of water = 0.01 g/(cm.s); gravitational acceleration = 980 cm/s². If the incoming water contains particles of diameter 25 μm (spherical and uniform), the removal efficiency of these particles is
questions.explanation:
Environmental Engineering | Water Treatment (Sedimentation)

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Flow rate \((Q) = 0.2\text{ m}^3/\text{s}\)
    • Basin dimensions: \(L = 32\text{ m},\ W = 8\text{ m},\ D = 4\text{ m}\)
    • Particle density \((\rho_p) = 2.5\text{ g/cm}^3\)
    • Water density \((\rho_w) = 1\text{ g/cm}^3\)
    • Dynamic viscosity \((\mu) = 0.01\text{ g/(cm}\cdot\text{s)}\)
    • Gravity \((g) = 980\text{ cm/s}^2\)
    • Particle diameter \((d) = 25\ \mu\text{m}\)
  • Aim: Calculate the removal efficiency of these particles.

3. Core Concepts:

  • Surface Overflow Rate (\(V_o\)): The critical settling velocity required for 100% removal.\[V_o = \dfrac{Q}{\text{Surface Area}} \]
  • Stokes' Law: Calculates the actual settling velocity (\(V_s\)) of discrete spherical particles in a laminar regime.\[V_s = \dfrac{g (\rho_p - \rho_w) d^2}{18\mu} \]
  • Removal Efficiency (\(\eta\)): \(\eta = \left( \dfrac{V_s}{V_o} \right) \times 100\%\)

4. Solution Method:

  1. Convert all units to standard SI units (kg, m, s) for strict unit discipline.
  2. Calculate the Surface Overflow Rate (\(V_o\)).
  3. Calculate the settling velocity (\(V_s\)) using Stokes' law.
  4. Calculate the efficiency ratio.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

Step 1: Unit Conversions

  • \(Q = 0.2\text{ m}^3/\text{s}\)
  • \(\rho_p = 2.5\text{ g/cm}^3 = 2500\text{ kg/m}^3\)
  • \(\rho_w = 1.0\text{ g/cm}^3 = 1000\text{ kg/m}^3\)
  • \(\mu = 0.01\text{ g/(cm}\cdot\text{s)} = 0.001\text{ kg/(m}\cdot\text{s)}\) (or Pa⋅s)
  • \(g = 980\text{ cm/s}^2 = 9.8\text{ m/s}^2\)
  • \(d = 25\ \mu\text{m} = 25 \times 10^{-6}\text{ m}\)

Step 2: Surface Overflow Rate (\(V_o\))

\[A_s = L \times W = 32\text{ m} \times 8\text{ m} = 256\text{ m}^2 \]\[V_o = \dfrac{Q}{A_s} = \dfrac{0.2}{256} = 7.8125 \times 10^{-4}\text{ m/s} \]

Step 3: Settling Velocity (\(V_s\))

\[V_s = \dfrac{9.8 \times (2500 - 1000) \times (25 \times 10^{-6})^2}{18 \times 0.001} \]\[V_s = \dfrac{9.8 \times 1500 \times 625 \times 10^{-12}}{0.018} = \dfrac{9.1875 \times 10^{-6}}{0.018} = 5.1042 \times 10^{-4}\text{ m/s} \]

Step 4: Removal Efficiency (\(\eta\))

\[\eta = \dfrac{V_s}{V_o} \times 100\% = \dfrac{5.1042 \times 10^{-4}}{7.8125 \times 10^{-4}} \times 100\% = 65.33\% \]

6. Final Answer:

Removal Efficiency \(= 65.33\%\) | Correct option: (B)

questions.title: GATE CE 2019 Set 1 | CE Q35
questions.subject: Surveying & Geomatics
questions.question: A survey line was measured to be 285.5 m with a tape having a nominal length of 30 m. On checking, the true length of the tape was found to be 0.05 m too short. If the line lay on a slope of 1 in 10, the reduced length (horizontal length) of the line for plotting of survey work would be
questions.explanation:
Geomatics Engineering | Surveying (Linear Measurements)

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Measured length \((L_m) = 285.5\text{ m}\)
    • Nominal tape length \((l_n) = 30\text{ m}\)
    • Tape error \(= 0.05\text{ m}\) too short \(\implies\) True tape length \((l_t) = 30 - 0.05 = 29.95\text{ m}\)
    • Slope \(= 1\text{ in }10\)
  • Aim: Determine the reduced horizontal length of the line.

3. Core Concepts:

  • Tape Correction: If a tape is too short, the measured distance is longer than the actual distance.\[\text{True Slope Length }(L_t) = L_m \times \left( \dfrac{l_t}{l_n} \right) \]
  • Slope Correction: To plot survey work, horizontal distance \((H)\) must be found.\[H = L_t \times \cos\theta \]Note: A slope of 1 in 10 in standard topography conventionally means \(\tan\theta = 1/10\).

4. Solution Method:

  1. Apply the correction for absolute length to find the true length along the slope.
  2. Determine \(\cos\theta\) from the given slope gradient.
  3. Multiply the true slope length by \(\cos\theta\) to obtain the horizontal projection.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

Step 1: Apply Tape Correction

\[L_t = 285.5 \times \left( \dfrac{29.95}{30} \right) = 285.5 \times 0.998333 = 285.024\text{ m} \]

Step 2: Slope Correction

Slope gradient is \(\tan\theta = \dfrac{1}{10}\).

\[\cos\theta = \dfrac{10}{\sqrt{10^2 + 1^2}} = \dfrac{10}{\sqrt{101}} \approx 0.995037 \]

Even if interpreting 1 in 10 as \(\sin\theta = 1/10\), \(\cos\theta = \sqrt{1 - 0.1^2} \approx 0.99498\), which yields an identical final rounded answer.

Step 3: Horizontal Reduced Length

\[H = L_t \times \cos\theta = 285.024 \times 0.995037 = 283.609\text{ m} \approx 283.6\text{ m} \]

6. Final Answer:

Horizontal Length \(= 283.6\) m | Correct option: (A)

questions.title: GATE CE 2019 Set 1 | CE Q36
questions.subject: Concrete & Steel Structures
questions.topic: Steel Tension, Compression Members & Plastic Analysis
questions.question:
A 16 mm thick gusset plate is connected to the 12 mm thick flange plate of an I-section using fillet welds on both sides as shown in the figure (not drawn to scale). The gusset plate is subjected to a point load of 350 kN acting at a distance of 100 mm from the flange plate. Size of fillet weld is 10 mm.

The maximum resultant stress (in MPa, round off to 1 decimal place) on the fillet weld along the vertical plane would be ________
questions.explanation:
Design of Steel Structures | Eccentric Welded Connections

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application / Analysis
  • Given Data:
    • Two vertical fillet welds on both sides of a 16 mm gusset plate.
    • Length of each weld \((d) = 500\text{ mm}\)
    • Size of weld \((s) = 10\text{ mm}\)
    • Point load \((P) = 350\text{ kN}\)
    • Eccentricity from weld plane \((e) = 100\text{ mm}\)
  • Aim: Determine the maximum resultant (equivalent) stress on the fillet weld.

3. Core Concepts:

  • Throat Thickness: \(t_t = 0.7 \times s\)
  • Eccentricity Perpendicular to Weld Plane: This load causes direct shear stress \((q)\) acting downwards and normal bending stress \((f_a)\) perpendicular to the throat plane.
  • IS 800:2007 (Cl. 10.5.10.1.1) Equivalent Stress: The maximum combined effect on the weld throat is checked using the von Mises yield criterion approach:\[f_e = \sqrt{f_a^2 + 3q^2} \]

4. Solution Method:

  1. Determine throat thickness and calculate the effective weld area to find direct shear stress \((q)\).
  2. Calculate the Section Modulus \((Z)\) of the weld group along the vertical plane.
  3. Calculate the bending moment \((M)\) and find the resulting normal stress \((f_a = M/Z)\).
  4. Calculate the equivalent stress \(f_e\) and round to one decimal place.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

Step 1: Properties of the Weld Group

  • Throat thickness: \(t_t = 0.7 \times 10\text{ mm} = 7\text{ mm}\)
  • Total weld area: \(A = 2 \times (d \times t_t) = 2 \times 500 \times 7 = 7000\text{ mm}^2\)
  • Section modulus of two vertical welds:\[Z = 2 \times \left( \dfrac{t_t \times d^2}{6} \right) = 2 \times \dfrac{7 \times 500^2}{6} = 583{,}333.33\text{ mm}^3 \]

Step 2: Direct Shear Stress (\(q\))

\[q = \dfrac{P}{A} = \dfrac{350 \times 10^3}{7000} = 50\text{ MPa} \]

Step 3: Normal Bending Stress (\(f_a\))

\[M = P \times e = 350 \times 10^3\text{ N} \times 100\text{ mm} = 35 \times 10^6\text{ N}\cdot\text{mm} \]\[f_a = \dfrac{M}{Z} = \dfrac{35 \times 10^6}{583{,}333.33} = 60\text{ MPa} \]

Step 4: Equivalent Resultant Stress (\(f_e\))

Using the IS 800:2007 equivalent stress formulation:

\[f_e = \sqrt{f_a^2 + 3q^2} = \sqrt{60^2 + 3(50)^2} \]\[f_e = \sqrt{3600 + 7500} = \sqrt{11100} = 105.356\text{ MPa} \approx 105.4\text{ MPa} \]

6. Final Answer:

Maximum Equivalent Stress \(= 105.4\) MPa | Accepted key range: 105.3 to 105.5
