questions.question:
The network of a small construction project awarded to a contractor is shown in the following figure. The normal duration, crash duration, normal cost, and crash cost of all the activities are shown in the table. The indirect cost incurred by the contractor is INR 5000 per day.

If the project is targeted for completion in 16 days, the total cost (in INR) to be incurred by the contractor would be ________
questions.explanation:
Construction Management | Project Crashing & Optimization

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application & Analysis
  • Given Data:
    • Project network with paths and activity details (Normal Duration \(t_n\), Crash Duration \(t_c\), Normal Cost \(C_n\), Crash Cost \(C_c\)).
    • Indirect Cost = INR 5000 / day.
    • Target project duration = 16 days.
  • Aim: Find the total cost (Direct + Indirect) incurred to complete the project in exactly 16 days.

3. Core Concepts:

  • Cost Slope: The rate of increase in direct cost per day of crashing an activity.\[\text{Cost Slope} = \dfrac{\text{Crash Cost} - \text{Normal Cost}}{\text{Normal Duration} - \text{Crash Duration}} \]
  • Critical Path: The longest continuous path in the network, dictating the overall project duration.
  • Crashing Strategy: To reduce project duration, always crash the critical activity (or combination of activities for parallel critical paths) that has the minimum total cost slope.
  • Total Cost: \(\text{Total Cost} = \text{Total Normal Cost} + \text{Total Crashing Cost} + (\text{Indirect Cost/day} \times \text{Duration})\)

4. Solution Method:

  1. Calculate the Cost Slope for all activities.
  2. Determine all network paths and identify the critical path(s) under normal conditions.
  3. Calculate the initial Total Direct Cost under normal conditions.
  4. Crash the network step-by-step, targeting minimum cost slopes, until the project duration reaches the 16-day target.
  5. Compute the final Total Cost.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

Step 1: Calculate Cost Slopes and Normal Direct Cost

  • P: \((25000 - 15000) / (6 - 4) = 10000 / 2 = 5000\) INR/day
  • Q: \((12000 - 6000) / (5 - 2) = 6000 / 3 = 2000\) INR/day
  • R: \((9500 - 8000) / (5 - 3) = 1500 / 2 = 750\) INR/day
  • S: \((10000 - 7000) / (6 - 3) = 3000 / 3 = 1000\) INR/day
  • T: \((9000 - 6000) / (3 - 2) = 3000 / 1 = 3000\) INR/day
  • U: \((6000 - 4000) / (2 - 1) = 2000 / 1 = 2000\) INR/day
  • V: \((28000 - 20000) / (4 - 2) = 8000 / 2 = 4000\) INR/day
  • Total Normal Direct Cost \(= \sum C_n = 15k + 6k + 8k + 7k + 6k + 4k + 20k = 66{,}000\) INR

Step 2: Identify Paths and Normal Duration

  • Path 1: \(P - Q - U - V \Rightarrow 6 + 5 + 2 + 4 = 17\) days
  • Path 2: \(P - R - T - V \Rightarrow 6 + 5 + 3 + 4 = \mathbf{18}\) days (Critical Path)
  • Path 3: \(P - S - V \Rightarrow 6 + 6 + 4 = 16\) days

Normal duration is 18 days. We must crash it by 2 days.

Step 3: Crashing Iteration 1 (18 days → 17 days)

  • Target the critical path: \(P - R - T - V\).
  • Available activities to crash with cost slopes: P (5000), R (750), T (3000), V (4000).
  • Activity R has the minimum cost slope (750 INR/day). Crash R by 1 day.
  • Cost incurred = 750 INR.
  • New Path lengths: P-Q-U-V = 17 days, P-R-T-V = 17 days, P-S-V = 16 days.

Step 4: Crashing Iteration 2 (17 days → 16 days)

Now we have two parallel critical paths: \(P - Q - U - V\) (17) and \(P - R - T - V\) (17). We must crash both simultaneously by 1 day. Valid options:

  • Crash common activity P: 5000 INR
  • Crash common activity V: 4000 INR
  • Crash parallel activities (R + Q): \(750 + 2000 = 2750\) INR
  • Crash parallel activities (R + U): \(750 + 2000 = 2750\) INR
  • Crash parallel activities (T + Q): \(3000 + 2000 = 5000\) INR

The minimum cost option is to crash R and Q (or R and U) together.
Cost incurred = 2750 INR.
New Path lengths: All three paths are now exactly 16 days. Target achieved!

Step 5: Compute Final Total Cost

  • Total Crashing Cost \(= 750 + 2750 = 3500\) INR
  • Total Direct Cost \(= 66{,}000 + 3{,}500 = 69{,}500\) INR
  • Total Indirect Cost \(= 16 \text{ days} \times 5000 \text{ INR/day} = 80{,}000\) INR
  • Total Cost \(= 69{,}500 + 80{,}000 = 1{,}49{,}500\) INR

6. Final Answer:

Total Cost \(= \mathbf{1{,}49{,}500}\) INR | Accepted key range: 149500 to 149500

questions.title: GATE CE 2019 Set 1 | CE Q38
questions.subject: Concrete & Steel Structures
questions.topic: Limit State Design of Beams & Slabs
questions.question: A box measuring 50 cm × 50 cm × 50 cm is filled to the top with dry coarse aggregate of mass 187.5 kg. The water absorption and specific gravity of the aggregate are 0.5% and 2.5, respectively. The maximum quantity of water (in kg, round off to 2 decimal places) required to fill the box completely is ________
questions.explanation:
Geotechnical Engineering / Concrete Technology | Aggregate Properties

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Box dimensions: \(L = 50\text{ cm},\ W = 50\text{ cm},\ H = 50\text{ cm}\)
    • Mass of dry coarse aggregate \((M_s) = 187.5\) kg
    • Water absorption of aggregate \(= 0.5\%\)
    • Specific gravity of aggregate \((G_s) = 2.5\)
  • Aim: Calculate the maximum quantity of water (in kg) required to completely fill the box.

3. Core Concepts:

The water required will fulfill two purposes:

  1. Water absorbed into the permeable pores of the dry aggregates (Water Absorption).
  2. Water filling the empty void spaces between the aggregate particles (Void Volume).
  • Volume of Box (\(V\)): \(V = V_s + V_v\) (Volume of Solid Aggregates + Volume of Voids)
  • True Volume of Solids: \(V_s = \dfrac{M_s}{G_s \times \rho_w}\)
  • Density of Water (\(\rho_w\)): \(1000\text{ kg/m}^3\)

4. Solution Method:

  1. Calculate the total geometrical volume of the box (\(V\)).
  2. Calculate the absolute volume occupied by the solid aggregates (\(V_s\)).
  3. Find the volume of voids in the box (\(V_v = V - V_s\)).
  4. Convert the void volume into the mass of water required to fill it.
  5. Calculate the mass of water absorbed by the aggregates.
  6. Sum both water masses to get the final total quantity.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

Step 1: Total Box Volume

\[V = 0.5\text{ m} \times 0.5\text{ m} \times 0.5\text{ m} = 0.125\text{ m}^3 \]

Step 2: Volume of Solid Aggregate

\[V_s = \dfrac{187.5\text{ kg}}{2.5 \times 1000\text{ kg/m}^3} = \dfrac{187.5}{2500} = 0.075\text{ m}^3 \]

Step 3: Volume and Mass of Water to Fill Voids

\[V_v = V - V_s = 0.125 - 0.075 = 0.050\text{ m}^3 \]\[M_{\text{voids}} = V_v \times \rho_w = 0.050\text{ m}^3 \times 1000\text{ kg/m}^3 = 50.00\text{ kg} \]

Step 4: Mass of Water Absorbed

\[M_{\text{absorbed}} = 0.5\%\text{ of }M_s = \dfrac{0.5}{100} \times 187.5 = 0.9375\text{ kg} \]

Step 5: Total Water Required

\[\text{Total Water} = M_{\text{voids}} + M_{\text{absorbed}} = 50.00 + 0.9375 = 50.9375\text{ kg} \approx 50.94\text{ kg} \]

6. Final Answer:

Total Water \(= 50.94\) kg | Accepted key range: 50.50 to 51.20

questions.title: GATE CE 2019 Set 1 | CE Q39
questions.subject: Structural Analysis & Mechanics
questions.question: A portal frame shown in figure (not drawn to scale) has a hinge support at joint P and a roller support at joint R. A point load of 50 kN is acting at joint R in the horizontal direction. The flexural rigidity, EI, of each member is 10⁶ kNm². Under the applied load, the horizontal displacement (in mm, round off to 1 decimal place) of joint R would be ________
questions.explanation:
Structural Analysis | Deflection of Frames

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application & Analysis
  • Given Data:
    • Portal frame with hinge at P and roller at R.
    • Member PQ (horizontal beam) length \(= 5\) m.
    • Member QR (vertical column) length \(= 10\) m.
    • Horizontal Point Load at R \(= 50\) kN.
    • Flexural Rigidity \((EI) = 10^6\text{ kNm}^2\).
  • Aim: Find the horizontal displacement at joint R in mm.

3. Core Concepts:

Castigliano's Second Theorem: The partial derivative of the total strain energy \((U)\) of a linearly elastic structure with respect to an applied load \((P)\) is equal to the displacement \((\Delta)\) in the direction of that load.

\[\Delta_R = \dfrac{\partial U}{\partial P} = \int \dfrac{M}{EI} \dfrac{\partial M}{\partial P}\, ds \]

where \(M\) is the internal bending moment written as a function of the generic variable load \(P\).

4. Solution Method:

  1. Apply a variable horizontal load \(F\) at the roller support R (where actual load is 50 kN).
  2. Compute the support reactions at P and R in terms of \(F\).
  3. Establish local coordinate systems for members QR and PQ and express the bending moment \(M(x)\) and \(M(y)\) in terms of \(F\).
  4. Find \(\dfrac{\partial M}{\partial F}\) for both members.
  5. Integrate over the lengths of both members to find the displacement.
  6. Substitute the actual load \(F = 50\text{ kN}\) into the final expression.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

Step 1: Reactions under load \(F\) at R

  • P is at \((0, 10)\), Q is at \((5, 10)\), R is at \((5, 0)\). Load \(F\) acts horizontally at R.
  • \(\sum M_P = 0 \Rightarrow V_R \times 5 - F \times 10 = 0 \Rightarrow V_R = 2F\) (Upwards)
  • \(\sum F_y = 0 \Rightarrow V_P = -2F\) (Downwards)
  • \(\sum F_x = 0 \Rightarrow H_P = -F\) (Leftwards)

Step 2: Bending Moment Equations

  • Member QR: Origin at R, variable \(y\) pointing upwards (\(0 \le y \le 10\)):
    \(M_{QR}(y) = F \cdot y\)    and    \(\dfrac{\partial M_{QR}}{\partial F} = y\)
  • Member PQ: Origin at P, variable \(x\) pointing rightwards (\(0 \le x \le 5\)):
    \(M_{PQ}(x) = V_P \cdot x = 2Fx\)    and    \(\dfrac{\partial M_{PQ}}{\partial F} = 2x\)

Step 3: Apply Castigliano's Theorem

\[\Delta_R = \int_0^{10} \dfrac{(Fy)(y)}{EI}\, dy + \int_0^{5} \dfrac{(2Fx)(2x)}{EI}\, dx \]\[ \Delta_R = \dfrac{F}{EI} \left[\int_0^{10} y^2\, dy + \int_0^{5} 4x^2\, dx \right] \]\[ \Delta_R = \dfrac{F}{EI} \left[\left( \dfrac{y^3}{3} \right)_0^{10} + \left( \dfrac{4x^3}{3} \right)_0^{5} \right] \]\[ \Delta_R = \dfrac{50}{10^6} \left[\dfrac{1000}{3} + \dfrac{4 \times 125}{3} \right] = \dfrac{50}{10^6} \left[\dfrac{1000 + 500}{3} \right] = \dfrac{50}{10^6} \times 500 = \dfrac{25000}{10^6}\text{ m} \]

Step 4: Unit Conversion to mm

\[\Delta_R = 0.025\text{ m} \times 1000\text{ mm/m} = 25.0\text{ mm} \]

6. Final Answer:

Horizontal displacement at R \(= 25.0\) mm | Accepted key range: 24.9 to 25.1

questions.title: GATE CE 2019 Set 1 | CE Q40
questions.subject: Environmental Engineering
questions.question: A sample of air analysed at 0°C and 1 atm pressure is reported to contain 0.02 ppm (parts per million) of NO₂. Assume the gram molecular mass of NO₂ as 46 and its volume at 0°C and 1 atm pressure as 22.4 litres per mole. The equivalent NO₂ concentration (in microgram per cubic meter, round off to 2 decimal places) would be ________
questions.explanation:
Environmental Engineering | Air Pollution Metrics

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Concentration of \(\text{NO}_2 = 0.02\) ppm
    • Temperature \(= 0^\circ\text{C}\), Pressure \(= 1\) atm
    • Gram molecular mass of \(\text{NO}_2\) \((M) = 46\) g/mol
    • Volume of 1 mole of gas at given conditions \((V_m) = 22.4\) L/mol
  • Aim: Convert the concentration from ppm to \(\mu\text{g/m}^3\).

3. Core Concepts:

  • Parts Per Million (ppm) by Volume: 1 ppm means 1 volume unit of pollutant per \(10^6\) volume units of air.
  • Conversion Formula (derived from the Ideal Gas Law):\[\text{Concentration } (\mu\text{g/m}^3) = \dfrac{\text{Concentration (ppm)} \times M \times 1000}{V_m} \]The multiplier of 1000 converts from mg/m\(^3\) to \(\mu\)g/m\(^3\).

4. Solution Method:

  1. Verify standard conditions: The volume of 1 mole is directly given as 22.4 L/mol (Standard Temperature and Pressure).
  2. Plug the values into the mass-to-volume conversion formula.
  3. Round off to two decimal places.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

Step 1: Apply Conversion Formula

\[C\ (\mu\text{g/m}^3) = C\text{ (ppm)} \times \dfrac{\text{Molecular Weight}}{\text{Molar Volume}} \times 1000 \]\[C = 0.02 \times \dfrac{46}{22.4} \times 1000 \]

Step 2: Computation

\[C = 0.02 \times 2.05357 \times 1000 = 41.07\ \mu\text{g/m}^3 \]

6. Final Answer:

\(C = 41.07\ \mu\text{g/m}^3\) | Accepted key range: 41.00 to 41.10

questions.title: GATE CE 2019 Set 1 | CE Q41
questions.subject: Environmental Engineering
questions.question: A 0.80 m deep bed of sand filter (length 4 m and width 3 m) is made of uniform particles (diameter = 0.40 mm, specific gravity = 2.65, shape factor = 0.85) with bed porosity of 0.4. The bed has to be backwashed at a flow rate of 3.60 m³/min. During backwashing, if the terminal settling velocity of sand particles is 0.05 m/s, the expanded bed depth (in m, round off to 2 decimal places) is ________
questions.explanation:
Environmental Engineering | Water Treatment (Filtration)

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application & Analysis
  • Given Data:
    • Initial Depth \((D_0) = 0.80\) m
    • Filter Area \((A) = 4\text{ m} \times 3\text{ m} = 12\text{ m}^2\)
    • Initial Porosity \((n_0) = 0.4\)
    • Backwash Flow Rate \((Q) = 3.60\text{ m}^3/\text{min}\)
    • Terminal Settling Velocity \((V_t) = 0.05\text{ m/s}\)
  • Aim: Find the expanded bed depth (\(D_e\)) during backwashing in meters.

3. Core Concepts:

  • Richardson-Zaki Equation: Relates the backwash (approach) velocity \((V_B)\), terminal settling velocity \((V_t)\), and the expanded porosity \((n_e)\).\[V_B = V_t \cdot (n_e)^{4.5} \]The exponent 4.5 is standard empirical practice in Environmental Engineering for mixed-regime backwash typical of sand filters.
  • Conservation of Solids: The total volume of solid grains remains constant before and during expansion.\[D_0(1 - n_0) = D_e(1 - n_e) \]

4. Solution Method:

  1. Calculate the backwash velocity \(V_B\) from the flow rate and area (ensure units are in m/s).
  2. Use the Richardson-Zaki equation to solve for the expanded porosity \(n_e\).
  3. Use the solid conservation principle to solve for the expanded bed depth \(D_e\).

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

Step 1: Calculate Backwash Velocity (\(V_B\))

\[Q = 3.60\text{ m}^3/\text{min} = \dfrac{3.60}{60}\text{ m}^3/\text{s} = 0.06\text{ m}^3/\text{s} \]\[V_B = \dfrac{Q}{A} = \dfrac{0.06}{12} = 0.005\text{ m/s} \]

Step 2: Calculate Expanded Porosity (\(n_e\))

\[V_B = V_t \cdot (n_e)^{4.5} \]\[0.005 = 0.05 \cdot (n_e)^{4.5} \]\[(n_e)^{4.5} = \dfrac{0.005}{0.05} = 0.1 \]\[n_e = (0.1)^{\dfrac{1}{4.5}} = (0.1)^{0.2222} \approx 0.5995 \approx 0.60 \]

Step 3: Calculate Expanded Depth (\(D_e\))

\[ D_e = D_0 \left[\dfrac{1 - n_0}{1 - n_e} \right] = 0.80 \left[\dfrac{1 - 0.40}{1 - 0.5995} \right] = 0.80 \left[\dfrac{0.60}{0.4005} \right] = 1.198\text{ m} \approx 1.20\text{ m} \]

6. Final Answer:

Expanded Bed Depth \(D_e = 1.20\) m | Accepted key range: 1.15 to 1.25

questions.title: GATE CE 2019 Set 1 | CE Q42
questions.subject: Environmental Engineering
questions.question: A wastewater is to be disinfected with 35 mg/L of chlorine to obtain 99% kill of micro-organisms. The number of micro-organisms remaining alive (Nₜ) at time t, is modelled by Nₜ = N₀e⁻ᵏᵗ, where N₀ is number of micro-organisms at t = 0, and k is the rate of kill. The wastewater flow rate is 36 m³/h, and k = 0.23 min⁻¹. If the depth and width of the chlorination tank are 1.5 m and 1.0 m, respectively, the length of the tank (in m, round off to 2 decimal places) is ________
questions.explanation:
Environmental Engineering | Wastewater Disinfection

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Chlorine dosage \(= 35\) mg/L (distractor since reaction rate \(k\) is given independently)
    • Target efficiency \(= 99\%\) kill
    • Chick's Law model: \(N_t = N_0\, e^{-kt}\)
    • Rate constant \((k) = 0.23\text{ min}^{-1}\)
    • Wastewater flow rate \((Q) = 36\text{ m}^3/\text{h}\)
    • Tank Depth \((D) = 1.5\) m, Width \((W) = 1.0\) m
  • Aim: Calculate the required length of the chlorination tank.

3. Core Concepts:

  • Chick's Law: Describes first-order kinetics for the disinfection (die-off) of microorganisms.\[\ln\left(\dfrac{N_t}{N_0}\right) = -kt \]where \(N_t/N_0\) is the fraction of microorganisms surviving.
  • Hydraulic Retention Time (\(t\)):\[t = \dfrac{\text{Volume }(V)}{\text{Flow Rate }(Q)} \]
  • Tank Volume: \(V = L \times W \times D\)

4. Solution Method:

  1. Convert the 99% kill requirement into the survival fraction (\(N_t/N_0\)).
  2. Use Chick's law to solve for the required contact time (\(t\)).
  3. Calculate the required tank volume by multiplying flow rate by contact time (ensuring matching time units).
  4. Solve for the unknown tank length (\(L\)) using the volume and given cross-sectional dimensions.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

Step 1: Find Contact Time (\(t\))

99% kill means 1% survive: \(\dfrac{N_t}{N_0} = 1 - 0.99 = 0.01\)

\[0.01 = e^{-0.23t} \]

Taking natural log on both sides:

\[\ln(0.01) = -0.23t \implies -4.60517 = -0.23t \]\[t = \dfrac{4.60517}{0.23} = 20.0225\text{ min} \]

Step 2: Calculate Required Volume (\(V\))

\[Q = \dfrac{36\text{ m}^3/\text{h}}{60\text{ min/h}} = 0.6\text{ m}^3/\text{min} \]\[V = Q \times t = 0.6\text{ m}^3/\text{min} \times 20.0225\text{ min} = 12.0135\text{ m}^3 \]

Step 3: Calculate Tank Length (\(L\))

\[V = L \times W \times D \]\[12.0135 = L \times 1.0\text{ m} \times 1.5\text{ m} \]\[L = \dfrac{12.0135}{1.5} = 8.009\text{ m} \approx 8.01\text{ m} \]

Note: Chlorine dosage is extraneous information here, as the rate constant \(k\) is given directly and independently.

6. Final Answer:

Tank Length \(L = 8.01\) m | Accepted key range: 7.95 to 8.15

questions.title: GATE CE 2019 Set 1 | CE Q43
questions.subject: Surveying & Geomatics
questions.question: A staff is placed on a benchmark (BM) of reduced level (RL) 100.000 m and a theodolite is placed at a horizontal distance of 50 m from the BM to measure the vertical angles. The measured vertical angles from the horizontal at the staff readings of 0.400 m and 2.400 m are found to be the same. Taking the height of the instrument as 1.400 m, the RL (in m) of the theodolite station is ________
questions.explanation:
Surveying | Trigonometric Levelling

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Analysis
  • Given Data:
    • Reduced Level (RL) of Benchmark (BM) \(= 100.000\) m
    • Horizontal distance to staff, \(D = 50\) m
    • Staff readings: \(h_1 = 0.400\) m and \(h_2 = 2.400\) m
    • Measured vertical angles to these readings are equal in magnitude.
    • Height of theodolite instrument (HI) \(= 1.400\) m
  • Aim: Calculate the RL of the theodolite station.

3. Core Concepts:

  • Trigonometric Levelling: In a theodolite, vertical angles are measured from the horizontal line of sight (line of collimation).
  • If the vertical angles to two different staff readings are identical in magnitude, one must be an angle of elevation (\(+\theta\)) and the other an angle of depression (\(-\theta\)).
  • Because the distances from the horizontal crosshair to the two staff readings are \(+D\tan\theta\) and \(-D\tan\theta\) respectively, the horizontal line of sight will hit exactly at the midpoint of these two staff readings.
  • \(\text{Central staff reading} = \dfrac{h_1 + h_2}{2}\)
  • \(\text{RL of Line of Collimation} = \text{RL of BM} + \text{Central Staff Reading}\)
  • \(\text{RL of Station} = \text{RL of Line of Collimation} - \text{Height of Instrument}\)

4. Solution Method:

  1. Find the exact point where the horizontal line of sight hits the levelling staff.
  2. Determine the RL of the Line of Collimation.
  3. Subtract the theodolite's height to find the ground elevation of the station.

Note: The 50 m horizontal distance is superfluous data meant to distract; it cancels out geometrically.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Find horizontal reading:\[h_{\text{center}} = \dfrac{0.400 + 2.400}{2} = 1.400\text{ m} \]
  2. Calculate RL of the Line of Collimation (staff is placed on the BM):\[\text{RL of Collimation} = 100.000\text{ m} + 1.400\text{ m} = 101.400\text{ m} \]
  3. Calculate RL of Theodolite Station:\[\text{RL of Station} = \text{RL of Collimation} - \text{HI} = 101.400\text{ m} - 1.400\text{ m} = 100.000\text{ m} \]

6. Final Answer:

RL of Station \(= 100.000\) m | Accepted key range: 100 to 100

questions.title: GATE CE 2019 Set 1 | CE Q44
questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.question: Consider the ordinary differential equation \( x^2 \dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2} - 2x\dfrac{dy}{dx} + 2y = 0 \). Given the values of y(1) = 0 and y(2) = 2, the value of y(3) (round off to 1 decimal place), is ________
questions.explanation:
Engineering Mathematics | Differential Equations

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Differential equation: \(x^2 \dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2} - 2x\dfrac{dy}{dx} + 2y = 0\)
    • Boundary conditions: \(y(1) = 0\) and \(y(2) = 2\)
  • Aim: Evaluate \(y(3)\) and round off to 1 decimal place.

3. Core Concepts:

  • Cauchy-Euler Equation: A linear homogeneous ODE with variable coefficients of the form \(ax^2y'' + bxy' + cy = 0\).
  • Solved by substituting \(y = x^m\), which transforms the equation into an auxiliary algebraic equation: \(am(m-1) + bm + c = 0\).

4. Solution Method:

  1. Formulate the characteristic equation.
  2. Find the roots \(m_1\) and \(m_2\).
  3. Write the general solution: \(y(x) = C_1 x^{m_1} + C_2 x^{m_2}\).
  4. Use the boundary conditions to find the constants \(C_1\) and \(C_2\).
  5. Substitute \(x = 3\) into the specific solution.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Characteristic Equation:
    Substitute \(y = x^m\), \(y' = mx^{m-1}\), \(y'' = m(m-1)x^{m-2}\):\[m(m-1) - 2m + 2 = 0 \implies m^2 - 3m + 2 = 0 \]
  2. Find Roots:\[(m-1)(m-2) = 0 \implies m_1 = 1,\ m_2 = 2 \]
  3. General Solution:\[y(x) = C_1 x + C_2 x^2 \]
  4. Apply Boundary Conditions:
    At \(x=1,\ y=0\):\[0 = C_1 + C_2 \implies C_1 = -C_2 \quad \cdots\text{(Eq. 1)} \]At \(x=2,\ y=2\):\[2 = 2C_1 + 4C_2 \implies C_1 + 2C_2 = 1 \quad \cdots\text{(Eq. 2)} \]Substituting Eq. 1 into Eq. 2:\[-C_2 + 2C_2 = 1 \implies C_2 = 1,\ C_1 = -1 \]Specific solution: \(y(x) = x^2 - x\)
  5. Evaluate at \(x = 3\):\[y(3) = (3)^2 - 3 = 9 - 3 = 6 \]

6. Final Answer:

\(y(3) = 6.0\) | Accepted key range: 5.9 to 6.1

questions.title: GATE CE 2019 Set 1 | CE Q45
questions.subject: Transportation Engineering
questions.question: Average free flow speed and the jam density observed on a road stretch are 60 km/h and 120 vehicles/km, respectively. For a linear speed-density relationship, the maximum flow on the road stretch (in vehicles/h) is ________
questions.explanation:
Transportation Engineering | Traffic Flow Theory

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Free flow speed, \(v_f = 60\) km/h
    • Jam density, \(k_j = 120\) veh/km
    • Linear speed-density relationship
  • Aim: Determine the maximum flow \(q_{\max}\) on the road stretch.

3. Core Concepts:

  • Greenshields Macroscopic Model: Assumes a linear relationship between speed (\(v\)) and density (\(k\)):\[v = v_f \left(1 - \dfrac{k}{k_j}\right) \]
  • Fundamental Traffic Equation: \(q = k \times v\)
  • Maximum Flow (\(q_{\max}\)): The parabolic \(q\)-\(k\) curve peaks at exactly half the jam density and half the free flow speed:\[q_{\max} = \dfrac{v_f \times k_j}{4} \]

4. Solution Method:

  1. Verify the model matches Greenshields (linear \(v\)-\(k\)).
  2. Directly apply the peak capacity formula.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

\[q_{\max} = \dfrac{60\text{ km/h} \times 120\text{ veh/km}}{4} = \dfrac{7200}{4} = 1800\text{ veh/h} \]

6. Final Answer:

\(q_{\max} = 1800\) veh/h | Accepted key range: 1800 to 1800

questions.title: GATE CE 2019 Set 1 | CE Q46
questions.subject: Transportation Engineering
questions.question: Traffic on a highway is moving at a rate of 360 vehicles per hour at a location. If the number of vehicles arriving on this highway follows Poisson distribution, the probability (round off to 2 decimal places) that the headway between successive vehicles lies between 6 and 10 seconds is ________
questions.explanation:
Transportation Engineering | Traffic Flow Theory

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Traffic volume/rate, \(\lambda = 360\) veh/h
    • Arrival distribution: Poisson
    • Headway bounds: \(t_1 = 6\) s and \(t_2 = 10\) s
  • Aim: Calculate the probability that the headway lies between 6 and 10 seconds.

3. Core Concepts:

  • Poisson Arrivals & Exponential Headways: If vehicle arrivals follow a discrete Poisson process, the time gaps (headways, \(h\)) between successive vehicles follow a continuous Exponential Distribution.
  • PDF: \(f(t) = \lambda e^{-\lambda t}\)
  • CDF: \(P(h < t) = 1 - e^{-\lambda t}\)
  • Probability between bounds: \(P(t_1 \le h \le t_2) = e^{-\lambda t_1} - e^{-\lambda t_2}\)

4. Solution Method:

  1. Convert the flow rate (\(\lambda\)) into consistent units (vehicles per second).
  2. Apply the exponential distribution formula for the given bounds.
  3. Round to 2 decimal places.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Convert Flow Rate to per second:\[\lambda = \dfrac{360\text{ veh/h}}{3600\text{ s/h}} = 0.1\text{ veh/s} \]
  2. Calculate Probability:\[P(6 \le h \le 10) = e^{-\lambda \times 6} - e^{-\lambda \times 10} = e^{-0.6} - e^{-1.0} \]
  3. Evaluate:\[e^{-0.6} \approx 0.5488, \quad e^{-1.0} \approx 0.3679 \]\[P = 0.5488 - 0.3679 = 0.1809 \approx 0.18 \]

6. Final Answer:

\(P(6 \le h \le 10) = 0.18\) | Accepted key range: 0.17 to 0.19

questions.title: GATE CE 2019 Set 1 | CE Q47
questions.subject: Transportation Engineering
questions.question: A parabolic vertical curve is being designed to join a road of grade +5% with a road of grade –3%. The length of the vertical curve is 400 m measured along the horizontal. The vertical point of curvature (VPC) is located on the road of grade +5%. The difference in height between VPC and vertical point of intersection (VPI) (in m, round off to the nearest integer) is ________
questions.explanation:
Transportation Engineering | Geometric Design

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Comprehension
  • Given Data:
    • Initial Grade, \(n_1 = +5\% = +0.05\)
    • Final Grade, \(n_2 = -3\% = -0.03\)
    • Length of vertical curve, \(L = 400\) m
  • Aim: Find the difference in height between the Vertical Point of Curvature (VPC) and the Vertical Point of Intersection (VPI).

3. Core Concepts:

  • Parabolic Vertical Curves: By standard highway design geometry, a parabolic curve is tangent to the initial grade at the VPC and tangent to the final grade at the VPT.
  • Location of VPI: The intersection of the two tangents (VPI) is located exactly halfway along the horizontal length of the curve.
    Horizontal distance from VPC to VPI \(= \dfrac{L}{2}\).
  • The elevation changes simply by following the straight tangent line (gradient \(n_1\)) for a distance of \(\dfrac{L}{2}\).

4. Solution Method:

  1. Identify the horizontal distance to the VPI.
  2. Multiply this horizontal distance by the initial gradient slope (\(n_1\)) to find the height difference.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Determine Horizontal Distance:\[X = \dfrac{L}{2} = \dfrac{400}{2} = 200\text{ m} \]
  2. Calculate Elevation Difference:\[\Delta H = n_1 \times X = 0.05 \times 200\text{ m} = 10\text{ m} \]

6. Final Answer:

\(\Delta H = 10\) m | Accepted key range: 10 to 10

questions.title: GATE CE 2019 Set 1 | CE Q48
questions.subject: Transportation Engineering
questions.question: Tie bars of 12 mm diameter are to be provided in a concrete pavement slab. The working tensile stress of the tie bars is 230 MPa, the average bond strength between a tie bar and concrete is 2 MPa, and the joint gap between the slabs is 10 mm. Ignoring the loss of bond and the tolerance factor, the design length of the tie bars (in mm, round off to the nearest integer) is ________
questions.explanation:
Transportation Engineering | Highway Pavements

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Tie bar diameter, \(d = 12\) mm
    • Working tensile stress, \(f_t = 230\) MPa (N/mm\(^2\))
    • Average bond strength, \(\tau_{bd} = 2\) MPa (N/mm\(^2\))
    • Joint gap \(= 10\) mm
  • Aim: Find the design length of the tie bars as per standard codes.

3. Core Concepts:

  • Tie Bars in Rigid Pavement (IRC:58): Tie bars keep the longitudinal joints tightly closed. They are not load transfer devices like dowel bars.
  • The length of the tie bar must be sufficient to develop the full tensile strength of the bar via bond strength with the concrete.
  • Development Length (\(L_d\)): The length needed on one side of the joint, derived by equating pull-out force to bond resistance:\[\dfrac{\pi}{4} d^2 f_t = \pi d L_d \tau_{bd} \implies L_d = \dfrac{d \cdot f_t}{4 \cdot \tau_{bd}} \]
  • Total Design Length (\(L\)): The bar must be embedded by \(L_d\) on both sides of the joint gap:\[L = 2L_d + \text{Joint Gap} = \dfrac{d \cdot f_t}{2 \cdot \tau_{bd}} + \text{Joint Gap} \]

4. Solution Method:

  1. Calculate the required development length \(L_d\) for one side.
  2. Multiply by 2 and add the joint gap.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Calculate Development Length (\(L_d\)):\[L_d = \dfrac{12 \times 230}{4 \times 2} = \dfrac{2760}{8} = 345\text{ mm} \]
  2. Calculate Total Tie Bar Length (\(L\)):\[L = 2(345) + 10 = 690 + 10 = 700\text{ mm} \]

6. Final Answer:

Tie Bar Length \(= 700\) mm | Accepted key range: 700 to 700

questions.title: GATE CE 2019 Set 1 | CE Q49
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question:
The hyetograph of a storm event of duration 140 minutes is shown in the figure.

The infiltration capacity at the start of this event (t = 0) is 17 mm/hour, which linearly decreases to 10 mm/hour after 40 minutes duration. As the event progresses, the infiltration rate further drops down linearly to attain a value of 4 mm/hour at t = 100 minutes and remains constant thereafter till the end of the storm event. The value of the infiltration index, φ (in mm/hour, round off to 2 decimal places), is ________
questions.explanation:
Hydrology | Infiltration & Runoff

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Analysis
  • Given Data:
    • Storm duration \(= 140\) min
    • Rainfall intensity (\(i\)) in 20-min intervals (mm/h): 4, 8, 15, 10, 8, 3, 1
    • Infiltration capacity (\(f_c\)) curve:
      • \(t = 0\) to \(40\) min: 17 to 10 mm/h
      • \(t = 40\) to \(100\) min: 10 to 4 mm/h
      • \(t > 100\) min: Constant at 4 mm/h
  • Aim: Calculate the \(\phi\)-index (in mm/h).

3. Core Concepts:

  • Actual Infiltration vs. Rainfall: Actual infiltration rate \(f(t) = \min(i(t),\ f_c(t))\).
  • Direct Runoff (\(R\)): Runoff occurs only when \(i(t) > f_c(t)\). Total runoff is the area between the hyetograph and the actual infiltration curve.
  • \(\phi\)-index: The constant, average infiltration rate during periods of rainfall excess such that the calculated runoff strictly equals the actual observed runoff:\[R = \sum (i_j - \phi) \cdot \Delta t \quad \text{for intervals where } i_j > \phi \]

4. Solution Method:

  1. Divide the storm into 20-minute (\(\dfrac{1}{3}\) hour) intervals.
  2. Determine the average \(f_c\) for each interval.
  3. Calculate actual runoff generated in each interval and sum to get total Direct Runoff (\(R\)).
  4. Formulate the \(\phi\)-index equation iteratively by guessing a range for \(\phi\) to determine which rainfall blocks actively produce runoff.
  5. Solve for \(\phi\).

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

Step 1: Calculate Runoff per Interval (\(\Delta t = 20\text{ min} = \dfrac{1}{3}\text{ h}\))

Interval (min)\(i\) (mm/h)Avg \(f_c\) (mm/h)\(i\) vs \(f_c\)Runoff (mm)
0 – 20415.25\(i < f_c\)0
20 – 40811.75\(i < f_c\)0
40 – 60159\(i > f_c\)\((15-9) \times \dfrac{1}{3} = 2\) mm
60 – 80107\(i > f_c\)\((10-7) \times \dfrac{1}{3} = 1\) mm
80 – 10085\(i > f_c\)\((8-5) \times \dfrac{1}{3} = 1\) mm
100 – 12034\(i < f_c\)0
120 – 14014\(i < f_c\)0

Total Runoff (\(R\)) \(= 2 + 1 + 1 = 4\) mm

Step 2: Calculate the \(\phi\)-index

Assume \(\phi\) lies between \(4\) mm/h and \(8\) mm/h. Therefore, only intervals with \(i \ge 8\) mm/h contribute to runoff:
Contributing intervals: 20–40 (\(i=8\)), 40–60 (\(i=15\)), 60–80 (\(i=10\)), 80–100 (\(i=8\)).

  • Effective rainfall duration: \(t_e = 4 \times \dfrac{1}{3} = \dfrac{4}{3}\) hours
  • Total effective rainfall: \(P_e = (8+15+10+8) \times \dfrac{1}{3} = \dfrac{41}{3}\) mm

Apply the \(\phi\)-index formula:

\[R = P_e - \phi \cdot t_e \]\[4 = \dfrac{41}{3} - \phi \left(\dfrac{4}{3}\right) \]

Multiply through by 3:

\[12 = 41 - 4\phi \implies 4\phi = 29 \implies \phi = \dfrac{29}{4} = 7.25\text{ mm/h} \]

Sanity check: \(7.25\) mm/h correctly falls in the assumed \((4, 8]\) range, validating the assumption.

6. Final Answer:

\(\phi\text{-index} = 7.25\) mm/h | Accepted key range: 7.20 to 7.30

questions.title: GATE CE 2019 Set 1 | CE Q50
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question:
Two water reservoirs are connected by a siphon (running full) of total length 5000 m and diameter of 0.10 m, as shown below (figure not drawn to scale).

The inlet leg length of the siphon to its summit is 2000 m. The difference in the water surface levels of the two reservoirs is 5 m. Assume the permissible minimum absolute pressure at the summit of siphon to be 2.5 m of water when running full. Given: friction factor f = 0.02 throughout, atmospheric pressure = 10.3 m of water, and acceleration due to gravity g = 9.81 m/s². Considering only major loss using Darcy-Weisbach equation, the maximum height of the summit of siphon from the water level of upper reservoir, h (in m, round off to 1 decimal place) is ________
questions.explanation:
Fluid Mechanics | Pipe Flow / Siphon

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application & Analysis
  • Given Data:
    • Total pipe length \((L) = 5000\) m
    • Pipe diameter \((d) = 0.10\) m
    • Inlet leg length to summit \((L_1) = 2000\) m
    • Head difference between reservoirs \((\Delta H) = 5\) m
    • Min. absolute pressure at summit \((P_{s,abs}/\gamma) = 2.5\) m of water
    • Friction factor \((f) = 0.02\)
    • Atmospheric pressure head \((P_{atm}/\gamma) = 10.3\) m of water
    • \(g = 9.81\) m/s\(^2\)
  • Aim: Find the maximum height of the summit from the upper reservoir water level \((h)\).

3. Core Concepts:

  • Darcy-Weisbach Equation for major head loss:\[h_f = \dfrac{f \cdot L \cdot v^2}{2 \cdot g \cdot d} \]
  • Total System Head Loss: For reservoirs connected by a pipe, the total head loss equals the difference in water surface elevations (\(\Delta H = 5\) m).
  • Bernoulli's Energy Equation between the upper reservoir surface and the summit — absolute pressure values must be used.

4. Solution Method:

  1. Use the total head loss to find the steady flow velocity (\(v\)) in the siphon.
  2. Apply Bernoulli's equation between the top reservoir surface and the siphon summit, tracking head loss incurred strictly within the inlet leg (\(L_1\)).
  3. Solve the resulting equation for the elevation of the summit (\(h\)).

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

Step 1: Calculate the flow velocity (\(v\))

\[\Delta H = \dfrac{f \cdot L \cdot v^2}{2 \cdot g \cdot d} \]\[5 = \dfrac{0.02 \times 5000 \times v^2}{2 \times 9.81 \times 0.10} = \dfrac{100\, v^2}{1.962} \]\[v^2 = \dfrac{5 \times 1.962}{100} = 0.0981\text{ m}^2/\text{s}^2 \implies v = 0.3132\text{ m/s} \]

Step 2: Calculate head loss in the inlet leg (\(h_{f1}\))

\[h_{f1} = \dfrac{f \cdot L_1 \cdot v^2}{2 \cdot g \cdot d} = \dfrac{0.02 \times 2000 \times 0.0981}{2 \times 9.81 \times 0.10} = \dfrac{3.924}{1.962} = 2.0\text{ m} \]

Step 3: Apply Bernoulli's Equation
Point 1 = upper reservoir surface (datum, \(z_1 = 0\), \(v_1 \approx 0\)); Point S = siphon summit (\(z_S = h\), \(v_S = v\)).

\[\dfrac{P_1}{\gamma} + \dfrac{v_1^2}{2g} + z_1 = \dfrac{P_S}{\gamma} + \dfrac{v_S^2}{2g} + z_S + h_{f1} \]\[10.3 + 0 + 0 = 2.5 + \dfrac{0.0981}{2 \times 9.81} + h + 2.0 \]\[10.3 = 2.5 + 0.005 + h + 2.0 = 4.505 + h \]\[h = 10.3 - 4.505 = 5.795\text{ m} \approx 5.8\text{ m} \]

6. Final Answer:

Maximum summit height \(h = 5.8\) m | Accepted key range: 5.7 to 5.9

questions.title: GATE CE 2019 Set 1 | CE Q51
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question: Consider a laminar flow in the x-direction between two infinite parallel plates (Couette flow). The lower plate is stationary and the upper plate is moving with a velocity of 1 cm/s in the x-direction. The distance between the plates is 5 mm and the dynamic viscosity of the fluid is 0.01 N·s/m². If the shear stress on the lower plate is zero, the pressure gradient, \( \dfrac{\partial p}{\partial x} \), (in N/m² per m, round off to 1 decimal place) is ________
questions.explanation:
Fluid Mechanics | Viscous Flow (Couette Flow)

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Analysis
  • Given Data:
    • Velocity of upper plate \((U) = 1\) cm/s \(= 0.01\) m/s
    • Distance between plates \((h) = 5\) mm \(= 0.005\) m
    • Dynamic viscosity \((\mu) = 0.01\) N⋅s/m\(^2\)
    • Shear stress on lower plate \((\tau_{y=0}) = 0\)
  • Aim: Calculate the pressure gradient \(\dfrac{\partial p}{\partial x}\) in N/m\(^2\) per m.

3. Core Concepts:

  • Navier-Stokes Equation for 1D Laminar Flow: For fully developed steady flow between parallel plates, pressure forces balance viscous shear forces:\[\mu \dfrac{\partial^2 u}{\partial y^2} = \dfrac{\partial p}{\partial x} \]
  • Newton's Law of Viscosity: \(\tau = \mu\, \dfrac{\partial u}{\partial y}\)

4. Solution Method:

  1. Integrate the governing differential equation twice to get the general velocity profile \(u(y)\).
  2. Apply boundary conditions: \(u(0)=0\) (stationary bottom plate) and \(u(h)=U\) (moving top plate) to find integration constants.
  3. Differentiate \(u(y)\) to find the shear stress expression \(\tau(y)\).
  4. Set \(\tau\) at \(y=0\) equal to 0 and solve for \(\dfrac{\partial p}{\partial x}\).

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

Integrating \(\dfrac{\partial^2 u}{\partial y^2} = \dfrac{1}{\mu}\dfrac{\partial p}{\partial x}\) twice:

\[u(y) = \dfrac{1}{2\mu} \dfrac{\partial p}{\partial x} y^2 + C_1 y + C_2 \]

Apply Boundary Conditions:

  1. At \(y=0,\ u=0 \implies C_2 = 0\)
  2. At \(y=h,\ u=U \implies C_1 = \dfrac{U}{h} - \dfrac{1}{2\mu}\dfrac{\partial p}{\partial x}h\)

Shear stress profile:

\[\tau(y) = \mu\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial y} = \dfrac{\partial p}{\partial x}y + \mu C_1 \]

Given \(\tau(0) = 0\):

\[\mu C_1 = 0 \implies C_1 = 0 \]

Substituting \(C_1 = 0\) into the second boundary condition:

\[0 = \dfrac{U}{h} - \dfrac{1}{2\mu}\dfrac{\partial p}{\partial x}h \implies \dfrac{\partial p}{\partial x} = \dfrac{2\mu U}{h^2} \]

Substituting values:

\[\dfrac{\partial p}{\partial x} = \dfrac{2 \times 0.01 \times 0.01}{(0.005)^2} = \dfrac{0.0002}{0.000025} = 8.0\text{ N/m}^3 \]

6. Final Answer:

\(\dfrac{\partial p}{\partial x} = 8.0\) N/m\(^3\) | Accepted key range: 7.9 to 8.1

questions.title: GATE CE 2019 Set 1 | CE Q52
questions.subject: Geotechnical Engineering (Soil)
questions.question: A reinforced concrete circular pile of 12 m length and 0.6 m diameter is embedded in stiff clay which has an undrained unit cohesion of 110 kN/m². The adhesion factor is 0.5. The Net Ultimate Pullout (uplift) Load for the pile (in kN, round off to 1 decimal place) is ________
questions.explanation:
Geotechnical Engineering | Deep Foundations

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Pile length \((L) = 12\) m
    • Pile diameter \((D) = 0.6\) m
    • Undrained cohesion \((c_u) = 110\) kN/m\(^2\)
    • Adhesion factor \((\alpha) = 0.5\)
  • Aim: Calculate the Net Ultimate Pullout (uplift) Load.

3. Core Concepts:

  • Gross vs. Net Pullout Capacity:
    • Gross Pullout Capacity \(=\) Skin friction resistance \((Q_s)\) + Self-weight of pile \((W_p)\)
    • Net Pullout Capacity \(= Q_s\) (self-weight cancels; pulling out purely relies on adhesive resistance)
  • Skin Friction Capacity in Clay (IS 2911 Part 1):\[Q_s = \alpha \cdot c_u \cdot A_s \]where \(A_s = \pi D L\) is the shaft surface area.

4. Solution Method:

Calculate the surface area of the pile shaft. Multiply it by the unit adhesion (\(\alpha c_u\)) to get the final net capacity.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

Step 1: Calculate surface area (\(A_s\))

\[A_s = \pi \cdot D \cdot L = \pi \times 0.6 \times 12 = 7.2\pi \approx 22.6195\text{ m}^2 \]

Step 2: Calculate skin friction / net pullout (\(Q_s\))

\[Q_s = \alpha \cdot c_u \cdot A_s = 0.5 \times 110 \times 22.6195 = 55 \times 22.6195 = 1244.1\text{ kN} \]

6. Final Answer:

Net Ultimate Pullout Load \(= 1244.1\) kN | Accepted key range: 1240.0 to 1250.0

questions.title: GATE CE 2019 Set 1 | CE Q53
questions.subject: Geotechnical Engineering (Soil)
questions.question: A granular soil has a saturated unit weight of 20 kN/m³ and an effective angle of shearing resistance of 30°. The unit weight of water is 9.81 kN/m³. A slope is to be made on this soil deposit in which the seepage occurs parallel to the slope up to the free surface. Under this seepage condition for a factor of safety of 1.5, the safe slope angle (in degree, round off to 1 decimal place) would be ________
questions.explanation:
Geotechnical Engineering | Slope Stability

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Comprehension / Application
  • Given Data:
    • Saturated unit weight \((\gamma_{sat}) = 20\) kN/m\(^3\)
    • Effective friction angle \((\phi') = 30^\circ\)
    • Unit weight of water \((\gamma_w) = 9.81\) kN/m\(^3\)
    • Condition: Seepage occurs parallel to slope, up to the free surface
    • Factor of Safety \((\text{FoS}) = 1.5\)
  • Aim: Determine the safe slope angle (\(\beta\)) in degrees.

3. Core Concepts:

  • Infinite Slope Stability: For cohesionless soils (\(c'=0\)) undergoing steady seepage parallel to slope up to the ground surface, effective stress drops and heavily reduces shear strength.
  • Formula:\[\text{FoS} = \left( \dfrac{\gamma_{sub}}{\gamma_{sat}} \right) \dfrac{\tan\phi'}{\tan\beta} \]where \(\gamma_{sub} = \gamma_{sat} - \gamma_w\)

4. Solution Method:

  1. Calculate the submerged unit weight (\(\gamma_{sub}\)).
  2. Rearrange the stability formula to isolate \(\tan\beta\).
  3. Substitute the given variables to solve for the safe slope angle \(\beta\).

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

Step 1: Determine submerged unit weight

\[\gamma_{sub} = \gamma_{sat} - \gamma_w = 20 - 9.81 = 10.19\text{ kN/m}^3 \]

Step 2: Apply the FoS equation

\[1.5 = \dfrac{10.19}{20} \cdot \dfrac{\tan 30^\circ}{\tan\beta} \]

Step 3: Solve for \(\beta\)

\[\tan\beta = \dfrac{10.19}{20 \times 1.5} \times \tan 30^\circ = \dfrac{10.19}{30} \times 0.57735 = 0.33967 \times 0.57735 = 0.1961 \]\[\beta = \arctan(0.1961) = 11.1^\circ \]

6. Final Answer:

Safe slope angle \(\beta = 11.1^\circ\) | Accepted key range: 10.8 to 11.3

questions.title: GATE CE 2019 Set 1 | CE Q54
questions.subject: Geotechnical Engineering (Soil)
questions.question:
A 3 m × 3 m square precast reinforced concrete segments to be installed by pushing them through an existing railway embankment for making an underpass as shown in the figure. A reaction arrangement using precast PCC blocks placed on the ground is to be made for the jacks.

At each stage, the jacks are required to apply a force of 1875 kN to push the segment. The jacks will react against the rigid steel plate placed against the reaction arrangement. The footprint area of reaction arrangement on natural ground is 37.5 m². The unit weight of PCC block is 24 kN/m³. The properties of the natural ground are: c = 17 kPa; φ = 25° and γ = 18 kN/m³. Assuming that the reaction arrangement has rough interface and has the same properties that of soil, the factor of safety (round off to 1 decimal place) against shear failure is ________
questions.explanation:
Geotechnical Engineering | Shallow Foundations (Sliding)

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Jacking Force \((F_{\text{drive}}) = 1875\) kN
    • Reaction footprint area \((A) = 37.5\) m\(^2\)
    • Unit weight of PCC block \((\gamma_{PCC}) = 24\) kN/m\(^3\)
    • Height of PCC block stack \((H) = 7.5\) m
    • Soil parameters: \(c = 17\) kPa, \(\phi = 25^\circ\), \(\gamma = 18\) kN/m\(^3\)
    • Interface: Rough, adopts soil properties (\(c_a = c,\ \delta = \phi\))
  • Aim: Calculate the Factor of Safety against shear failure (sliding).

3. Core Concepts:

  • Sliding Resistance:\[F_{\text{resist}} = c_a \cdot A + N \cdot \tan(\delta) \]
  • Factor of Safety (Sliding):\[\text{FoS} = \dfrac{F_{\text{resist}}}{F_{\text{drive}}} \]

4. Solution Method:

  1. Determine the total dead weight (\(N\)) of the reaction block.
  2. Compute the sliding resistance at the base using Mohr-Coulomb failure criteria for soil-concrete interfaces.
  3. Divide resisting force by the jacking (driving) force.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

Step 1: Calculate normal force (\(N\))

\[\text{Volume} = A \times H = 37.5 \times 7.5 = 281.25\text{ m}^3 \]\[N = 281.25 \times 24 = 6750\text{ kN} \]

Step 2: Calculate sliding resistance (\(F_{\text{resist}}\))
Since the base is rough: \(c_a = 17\) kN/m\(^2\), \(\delta = 25^\circ\)

\[F_{\text{resist}} = c_a A + N\tan(\delta) = (17 \times 37.5) + (6750 \times \tan 25^\circ) \]\[F_{\text{resist}} = 637.5 + (6750 \times 0.4663) = 637.5 + 3147.57 = 3785.07\text{ kN} \]

Step 3: Calculate Factor of Safety

\[\text{FoS} = \dfrac{3785.07}{1875} = 2.02 \approx 2.0 \]

6. Final Answer:

\(\text{FoS} = 2.0\) | Accepted key range: 1.8 to 2.1

questions.title: GATE CE 2019 Set 1 | CE Q55
questions.subject: Geotechnical Engineering (Soil)
questions.question: A square footing of 4 m side is placed at 1 m depth in a sand deposit. The dry unit weight (γ) of sand is 15 kN/m³. This footing has an ultimate bearing capacity of 600 kPa. Consider the depth factors: d_q = d_γ = 1.0 and the bearing capacity factor: N_γ = 18.75. This footing is placed at a depth of 2 m in the same soil deposit. For a factor of safety of 3.0 as per Terzaghi’s theory, the safe bearing capacity (in kPa) of this footing would be ________
questions.explanation:
Geotechnical Engineering | Bearing Capacity

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Analysis
  • Given Data:
    • Square footing, width \((B) = 4\) m
    • Dry sand (\(c = 0\)), unit weight \((\gamma) = 15\) kN/m\(^3\)
    • Depth factors \(d_q = d_\gamma = 1.0\)
    • Bearing capacity factor \(N_\gamma = 18.75\)
    • At depth \(D_{f1} = 1\) m: Ultimate bearing capacity \(q_{u1} = 600\) kPa
  • Aim: Calculate the Safe Bearing Capacity at depth \(D_{f2} = 2\) m with FoS \(= 3.0\) as per Terzaghi's theory.

3. Core Concepts:

  • Terzaghi's Bearing Capacity Equation (Square Footing, sand \(c=0\)):\[q_u = \gamma D_f N_q + 0.4\, \gamma B N_\gamma \]
  • Gross vs. Net Safe Bearing Capacity:
    • Net Ultimate: \(q_{nu} = q_u - \gamma D_f\)
    • Net Safe: \(q_{ns} = q_{nu}/\text{FoS}\)
    • Gross Safe: \(q_{\text{safe}} = q_{ns} + \gamma D_f\) (rigorous approach)
    • Alternatively (textbook shortcut): \(q_{\text{safe}} = q_u / \text{FoS}\)

4. Solution Method:

  1. Use data from depth 1 (1 m) to back-calculate the unknown bearing capacity factor \(N_q\).
  2. Use the derived \(N_q\) to compute the new ultimate bearing capacity (\(q_{u2}\)) at depth 2 (2 m).
  3. Apply the FoS to calculate the safe bearing capacity.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

Step 1: Back-calculate \(N_q\) from Depth 1

\[q_{u1} = \gamma \cdot D_{f1} \cdot N_q + 0.4 \cdot \gamma \cdot B \cdot N_\gamma \]\[600 = (15 \times 1 \times N_q) + (0.4 \times 15 \times 4 \times 18.75) \]\[600 = 15N_q + 450 \implies 15N_q = 150 \implies N_q = 10 \]

Step 2: Calculate Ultimate Bearing Capacity at Depth 2 (\(D_{f2} = 2\) m)

\[q_{u2} = (15 \times 2 \times 10) + (0.4 \times 15 \times 4 \times 18.75) = 300 + 450 = 750\text{ kPa} \]

Step 3: Calculate Safe Bearing Capacity

Rigorous Net Method:

\[q_{nu2} = q_{u2} - \gamma D_{f2} = 750 - 30 = 720\text{ kPa} \]\[q_{ns} = \dfrac{720}{3} = 240\text{ kPa} \]\[q_{\text{safe}} = q_{ns} + \gamma D_{f2} = 240 + 30 = 270\text{ kPa} \]

Alternative Shortcut Method:

\[q_{\text{safe}} = \dfrac{q_{u2}}{\text{FoS}} = \dfrac{750}{3} = 250\text{ kPa} \]

Note: The official GATE key accepts either 250 kPa or 270 kPa.

6. Final Answer:

Safe Bearing Capacity \(= 270\) kPa (rigorous) or \(250\) kPa (shortcut) | Accepted key range: 250 to 250 or 270 to 270
